headline: CANTON CRISIS.
text:
Situation

barbers, Northerners, who had trekked in all the way from Sheklung (about 70 miles) decided to finish their journey with a free ride on the train.

This morning they were prosecuted by Mr. W. Cuff, traffic inspector, for not paying their fare from Shatin.

Admitting that they had no money and expressing a wish to return home via Shanghai, the men told His Worship (Mr. E. W. Hamilton) that they had walked all the way from Sheklung and at Shatin had boarded the train as they felt they could walk no more. A fine of $5 each, or seven days, was imposed.

headline: TROOPS ON THE MOVE.
text:
On all three railways entering Canton, large movements are proceeding.

"The situation is most grave. Fighting is believed to be imminent."

headline: STUDENT PARADE.
text:
To demonstrate their sympathy with the Shanghai rioters, hundreds of students held a mass parade yesterday afternoon, shouting "Down with Imperialism and "forgivers," when they marched past Shameen.

It has been stated that the Maritime Customs non-Chinese staff were called back to Shameen for safety about 2 p.m. until the parade was over.

Shannon's gates were closed but crowds of residents watched the proceedings from inside. The Police were armed and a picket of bluejackets was landed on the island.

When the parade was passing the French Bridge, the French commission police treated it non-relatively, taking little or no notice.

So-called cadets are again active with anti-foreign propaganda.

headline: FIGHTING STARTED?
text:
Reports have reached Canton of rival outposts having opened fire at one another in the East River district. The troops concerned are said to be those of General Yang. Hsi-man, commander-in-chief of the non-Cantonese mercenaries, and General Hsu Shungchi, commander-in-chief of the Kuomintang forces.

Troops are also on the move in the North River region.

The Yunnanese have been given a taste of the civil opposition the Soviets are stirring up against them. On the advice of "Red" Kuomintang Labourites, locomotive drivers have deserted the train services.

Yunnanese detachments are camping at the Railway Station. Anti-Communist staff officers have been trying to round up the skilled labour of the Canton-Samshui and Fatshan railways to run the trains on the Canton-Kowloon line (Chinese section). Heavy field-guns, weapons of all kinds, munitions and war waggons were transferred, this morning from Shekwaiting to the Canton-Kowloon Station (to the east of Canton) as the Communists may come from that direction).

The Communists are rallying at and around Honam where they have been mobilising, ostensibly, as a jumping-off point for an attack on the mercenary non-Cantonese headquarters in Canton. Their press announces that General Hsu will soon be back in Canton when their party will immediately "nationalise" the electric light and waterworks plant.

Refugees are crowding the Hongkong-bound boats and much property and valuables are, as usual, finding their way into Shameen. The eastern outskirts of the city are full of Yunnanese patrols and martial law is still in force.

People coming into Hongkong from the East River district report considerable alarm over the recent trend of events. Two EMPRESS DELAYED. The “Empress of Australia” has been delayed by 6am and will now arrive in Hongkong at 8:00 a.m. to microw Friday morning.

Another accident has occurred in connection with the Abbott School of Aviation. One of the new aeroplanes which has been flying often over the City is now lying wrecked in a swamp in the New Territories.

This latest mishap is all the more regrettable as it has taken place during the absence of Mr. H. W. Abbott, who left for Shanghai by the s.s. "Malwa" last Friday on business connected with the inauguration of a passenger and air mail service.

Details of the accident as given in a police report this morning are that a mechanic who had been an

assistant in the School took the machine out of the matshed. i.o Kowloon City and flew a distance of 30 miles when he crashed in a swamp at Lokmachau. The machine was badly damaged, but the pilot escaped injury and returned to Kowloon by motor car. The descent of the aeroplane into the swamp was witnessed by the Lokmachau Police. The students then stated that they desired to parade through the Legation Quarter, and after a discussion they sent four delegates to see the Doyen. The machine, which is a Curtiss plane named the “Oriols” and brought from Manila after the inauguration ceremony of the School in January, was removed by some person on Tuesday afternoon, the watchman placed at the shed raising no objection as he thought that the man had authority to do so. headline: NEW TELEPHONE CO. DIRECTORS.
text:
COMMÉNT IN COUNCIL.

Referring to an article appearing in yesterday's "Hongkong Daily Press" the Colonial Secretary at this afternoon's Legislative Council meeting stated that the action of the hon. member representing the Chamber of Commerce in the seconding the resolution in regard to the formation of the telephone Company had been criticised. It had been stated that the hon. member had acted wrongly in that he was interested in the proposed company. As the Government had been in close communication with the Chamber of Commerce throughout the negotiations he (the Colonial Secretary) thought it was entirely proper that the honor member should have seconded. He would gain nothing by seconding just as he would lose nothing by refraining from speaking or voting. He had been asked by the Government to express the views of the unofficial members. The Colonial Secretary termed the attack as wholly undeserved and showing a lack of knowledge of the facts. It was an attack which should be immediately resisted.

His Excellency the Governor also had a few strong remarks to make on the question. He said he had too high an opinion of the common sense of the inhabitants to suppose that anyone of them would be interested in or attach importance to the scurrilous attacks of an anonymous slanderer. The Council was familiar with the story of Justice Maule on the question of anonymous attacks. It could not be applied to printed passages in newspapers but the principle was sound. text:

Diplomatic Body's Decision To-day.

The Shanghai riots continue to be the chief topic in the news and their effects are being felt as far afield as Peking and Canton.

The students, this afternoon, proceeded to the Waichaopu: "where Minister Shen, Jnai-lip saw their representatives. He pointed out that the Government had already lodged a protest with the Powers and had sent Commissioners to Shanghai.

headline: "Explicit Protests."
parent_headline: THE SHANGHAI RIOTS. / PEKING STUDENTS ABANDON PARADE.
text:
A. Note, dated June 1., though hunded to the Italian Minister this afternoon, says:—

“I have the honour to draw the most serious attention of your Excellency to the unhappy facts following, which occurred on May 30, in the International Concession, Shanghai. Following the arrest of students and acts of violence towards Chinese workers, several of whom were wounded, a certain number of students from the different universities at Shanghai proceeded on the afternoon of May 30, to the Police Station of the International Concession as a protest and made speeches. The armed intervention of the police led to more than 40 students being arrested, four being killed outright, six seriously wounded, of whom two succumbed a little while afterwards, and 17 were slightly wounded, three of whom, however, died after. On learning with emotion of the above facts, I beg to remark that whatever might have been the character of the demonstration by the students, who are young men of good families and full of patriotism and unarmed, they should not have been treated as ordinary malefactors, but instead of calming them by appropriate means, the police had recourse to extreme mis翅，which are essentially condemned by humanity and justice. “Consequently, I find it absolutely necessary to address to your Excellency the most explicit protests, while reserving the right, when further reports giving complete details are received, to formulate all claims which may result from this deplorable incident for which the authorities of the Concession are entirely responsible.” “Further beg your Excellence to bring what has exceeded to the knowledge of the Minister on the

been arrested, and to act in concert with the special Commissioners for Foreign Affairs there to prevent on eventual, recurrence of similar incidents.

headline: Japanese Press Comment TOKYO. Tune 3.
parent_headline: THE SHANGHAI RIOTS. / PEKING STUDENTS ABANDON PARADE.
text:
This morning's papers in their leading articles comment upon the Shanghai situation, the general opinion being that the situation has been caused by the (ommunistic influence working on the anti-foreign sentiment bred by the unilateral treaties between China and the Powers.

Whilst sympathising with China's position, the papers emphasise that the present action frustrates rather than helps the cancelling of extraterritoriality.

The Diplomatic Body are meeting tomorrow, when it is understood they will discuss the Shanghai affair, and probably despatch a reply to the Walchiaopu Note immediately afterwards.

headline: Further Clashes.

text:
Further clashes have occurred in the central districts. Up to the present 21 strikers have been killed and 65 wounded.

Armoured cars have been rushed to the western district, which the concentrating rioters are finding a useful base for their operations against the Settlements.

At present there does not appear to be any ground on which to compose the differences owing to the foreigners' determination to suppress the riots, while the Chinese are too excited to listen to calm

The arrival of fresh batches of trerzled students reinforces the waverels.

headline: Women Injured.
parent_headline: THE SHANGHAI RIOTS. / PEKING STUDENTS ABANDON PARADE.
text:
The anti-foreign strike is spreading. All the foreign mills are now involved, also the telephones, water works, municipal electricity department, and some of the foreign newspapers.

The Municipal Council has succeeded in maintaining the public services by means of other labour.

A mob of 3,000 this morning attacked the Japanese iceworks: The police guards fired on the rioters, killed one and wounding five.

The attacks on individual foreigners continue. The rioters stoned tram cars and injured a number of women.

Many students from other centres are arriving at Shanghai. Four platoons of British blue-jackets and marines are being landed this evening and a similar number to-morrow morning.

headline: DEMANDS REFUSED.
text:
Japan Refuses To Consider Resolution.

Tokio.• June 5

The Foreign Office declined to consider a resolution presented by Chinese students yesterday demanding, inter alia, the replacement of the Japanese Consuls-General in Shanghai and Tsingtao, compensation for the Shanghai casualties, punishment of the guilty, abolition of extraterritoriality and retrocession of leased territory.

Some Policemen Strike.

About 400 Chinese of the Settlement police lower ranks are absent without leave.

The absentees form less than 20 per cent sof the Chinese on the police force.

Tokyo, June 5. Chinese students this afternoon presented a resolution to the Foreign Office demanding inter alia replacement of the Japanese Consul-Generals at Shanghai and Tsingtao, compensation for the casualties." punishment of the guilty abolition of extraterritoriality, retrocession of the released territory, and cancellation of the Taonan-fu and Tsitsihar Railway construction contract. The Foreign Office has replied that it is impossible to consider the demands.

The Foreign Office has sent a further note to the diplomats saying that there are further reports of the police firing while the arrested men have not all been freed as requested in the first note.

The Foreign Office again requests that most urgent instructions be sent to the consular authorities at Shanghai immediately to order, cessation of the practice of firing.

headline: Japan Waits.
text:
The Navy Office has postponed the departure of the Tatsuta mentioned yesterday pending further developments in Shanghai.

Yesterday's cables stated that the small Japanese cruiser Tatsuta was sailing from Sasebo for Shanghai with 200 marines aboard. also that the U.S.S. Jason, with 300 marines had sailed from Cavite to Shanghai and would arrive on Sunday.

Telegram Dislocation: Senders of telegrams are informed that telegrams to Shanghai are accepted at senders' risk only.

headline: Earlier Cables.
text: The Chamber of Commerce has decided against a general strike but advocated the boycott of the goods and currency of the countries concerned in the Shanghai affair, and the withdrawal of deposits from their banks. The American and Chinese staffs of the Y.M.C.A. and other American Missionary institutions have passed a resolution expressing the opinion that the evidence so far does not show any ground that the firing by the police was necessary.

headline: Tsingtao Parallel
text:
Mail reports of the Japanese Mill Strike at Taingtao last week show that the Chinese police were unable to suppress the riots until they fired on the strikers

The Shanghai and Tsingtao cases are strikingly parallel, but the Chinese have ignored the Tsingtao incident.

Strike circulars to-day call on domestic servants to walk out. Unemployed Russians, Boy Scouts, women and foreign volunteers are minimising the effects of the strike. As regards Foreigners, the food situation is merely inconvenient; whereas the poorer Chinese are beginning to feel the pinch of hunger and the danger is looming up of their looting provision shops.

text:
The small steamer Bataan recently launched by Messrs Balley & Co., Ltd., for Teodoro Yangco of Manila sailed for that port on Thursday after undergoing her official trials.

The Bataan is a steel twin screw passenger and cargo ferry boat for service between Manila and the province of Bataan at the Northern side of Manila Bay.

The vessel is 141 feet long, built under Lloyds survey and Huted with an oil fired boiler and two sets of high speed triple expansion engines having independent pump. headline: CHINA'S FATE.
text:
CIVIL WAR PLAN.

Much attention has been attracted to a statement by the Washington correspondence of the Associated Press declaring that he possesses information pointing to direct Soviet participation, in the impending armed struggle for the control of the whole of China. Preparations have already been made, contemplating a civil war in the northern provinces on an extensive scale which will dwarf the present outbreaks in the sour

The correspondent states that ultimately the struggle is likely

to approximate to the Russo-Japanese war.

The actual campaigning will be carried on by General Feng Yu-hsiang and General Chang Tso-lin but supplies will be furnished by Moscow and Tokyo.

The correspondent adds that considerable quantities of arms and amputation have crossed the frontier from Russia while Russian instructors are co-operating with General Feng's officers in Mongolia.

Up to the present American officials have withheld comment.

headline: DEATH AT HOME. / RETIRED HONGKONG INSPECTOR.
text:
News has been received of the death of Mr. W. C. Ford, a former Inspector of Police in Hongkong, at his home near Bristol on April 23. The late Mr. Ford joined the Hongkong Police Force in September 1882, and retired on pension in January 1905. At the time of his retirement he was in charge of work in connection with ricshas and weights and measures.

The deceased, who was 66 years of age, leaves a widow and two children—a son and a daughter—both of whom are married.

headline: GANG ON ROOF. / ARMED ROBBERS CHASED. / ONE MAN BHOT.
text:
A gang of three armed robbers took to the roof of No 84 Wyndham Street at 2.30 this morning when the neighbourhood rang with the sound of police whistles. A Weihaiwei constable gave chase and stopped the escape of one of the men by shooting him in the leg. The injured man is now in hospital. Late this afternoon I was informed that the Yunnanese mercenary headquarters in Canton is considering or has even gone to the extent of suggesting to the Consular body that steps be taken to protect foreigners from stray shots which may fall into Shameen (a British and French concession) and Tungshan (a suburb to the east of Canton where many Europeans and

strike is possible. Telegraphic communication with Hongkong is suspended.

Reuter's cable was despatched via London and must therefore mean that fighting started on Thursday evening

Up to 5 p.m. yesterday (Friday) when the night-boats left Canton, no fighting had occurred. The "China Mail's" Canton correspondent is certain on this point. His intelligence is borne out by the advice received by one of the Colony's leading mercantile houses from their Canton Office.

If fighting had actually started even as late as last night, wireless messages would have got through to the Naval authorities by now. No such report had come down when the “China Mail” made inquiries.

The first news of the general strike seem only too true. According to one of the best informed gentlemen in the Colony, the strike may not be directed principally against the Yunnanese but is also a move sympathetic to the strikers in Shanghai.

headline: A STATE OF WAR.
text:
CANTON FOREIGNERS DANGER.

LATEST POSITION.

Communist Strike

General

Anxiety is felt regarding the safety of foreigners in Canton and Shameen should indiscriminate firing break out and the watchful presence of warships is desired.

Begins:

Americans have residences). There is no secret made of the fact that the anti-Communists are hourly expecting attack from either direction, involving danger to both places.

British and American residents in Tungshan are seriously considering a request that gunboats be stationed to the east of Canton in case of emergency.

Tungshan is in close proximity to Taishatau and the terminus of the Canton-Kowloon Railway. Any offensive from the direction of the East River or this railway, or an attack on the heights overlooking Canton city would mean stray shots falling into Tungshan.

When the drive against Lung Chai-kwang was made years ago, Canton was subjected to firing from points further out than Shameen and a night watchman on the concession was hit by a ricochet. It is feared that something similar may happen but the danger from this side is not so great.

headline: EARLIER NEWS
text:
To-day, the outward position was one of stalemate. The mercenaries have given the impression that they will not start fighting unless attacked and, meanwhile, will keep their hold on the city.

On the other hand, the Communistic element of the Kuomintang is resorting to a general economic strike in Canton city, to starve out the non-Cantonese troops by cutting off all communication.

I have already reported the stoppage on the three railways entering Canton. Since then, the cross-river ferries, both native craft and motor-boats have been "got at" by Communist labourites. To day a cargo-coolie strike is threatened and it may not be long if even the essential services are suspended. If Canton was economically isolated, the mercenaries could still carry on by commanding supplies. Such a stoppage would seriously inconvenience everybody, including the foreign communities. There are some who predict that the economic strike has as its object not so much the staying out of the anti-Communists but rather the holding-up of the city's commerce so that the merchants will be according to the cedent when the Corporate war lords had to be bought out to prevent bloodshed and destruction. It is felt that fighting may even be averted at this moment if the merchants and bourgeois will come forward to negotiate, by payment, of course, for the Yunnanese and Kwangsi-ites to vacate the city. With trade as it is, money will not be so easily found as in previous instances.

Inquiries in Hongkong this morning tended to show that the report of the cargo stoppage is substantiated by the river-boats not accepting cargo for Canton during the week-end. Yesterday's and last night's steamers were full of people from Canton.

headline: WHO WILL WIN?
text:
FIGHT TO A FINISH.

Startling events which took place in Canton yesterday portend a fight to the finish between the alien militarists and the Cuntonese Reds.

headline: Foreigners Warncd
text:
(Frôm Our Own Corréspondent.)

Canton Sunday 2:45 p.m. Yesterday's action of the gunboats has brought on a real state of war. All Saturday night till the small hours of this morning and to day, there has been intermittent sniping from both sides.

Shameen is in little or no danger as the shots are not falling in that direction. But there is no telling what may happen to Europeans in or outside the city. "Consuls have warned their subjects to find shelter in Shameen or leave" Canton, and some of the girls at St. Hilda's School (near the East Parade ground) sailed for Hongkong "to-day. Other residents in Tungshan have left for Shameen.

After the gunboats and armed launches had passed out into the Back Reach, the Yunanese began to take up positions behind sandbag barricades on the Western and Central Bund. Snipers were busy on both sides of the river and several proved their marksmanship. One Yunnanese post was close by the Tung On S. S. Co.'s wharf. When the s.s. Sai On went alongside this morning, the position was obscured by the vessel. The mercenaries accordingly left that post but returned when the steamer sailed shortly after 3 o'clock and re-opened fire at the opposite bank. On the other side, the Communists had their points of vantage from which they replied to the rifles on the city side. At most only two or three rounds could have been fired from artillery and both sides used rifles and measers.

headline: Forlorn Hopes
text:
In the small hours of this morning (about 2 a.m.) the Communists sent out a forlorn hope to land in Canton. They embarked in the night in several fast launches from Honam and crossed the river under cover of Dutch Folly Island in the middle of the river. Before they had reached the Bund, they were sighted by the Yunnanese sentinels. Guards were called out from the vicinity. The launches used machine guns and the mercenaries on the Bund replied with mausers. Eventually the launches were driven off. This morning bodies were seen in the "river and it is believed that some of the attacking party were killed. The Yunnanese immediately withdrew their dead and wounded.

About 410 a.m. the attack was repeated but further down the river. This was also unsuccessful and the Communists retreated very quickly.

headline: Housetop Ambush.
text:
Carrying the fight into enemy territory, the Yunnanese sallied across the river at 5:35 a.m. There were only about forty of them and they ventured out into the river in small commandeered rowing boats. It was light then but I could not follow their movements as they were hidden behind shipping, having zig-zagged as soon as they started. When they returned about an hour later, the commander told me that they had reached some Honam steps but had not landed as they had spotted. Communists in ambush on housetops! This is given for what it is worth.

During the day, both sides spotted away at one another. The Bund was deserted and the Honam front was lined with sandbags and nothing else. The firing resembled the letting off of firecrackers, by lads in Hongkong streets after the first flush of China New Year. I saw at least two Yunnanese dead carried away and seven wounded. I cannot say what casualties there were on the Honam side as cross-river traffic has ceased on account of the general strike. Inside the city and in the western suburb people were walking about quite calmly.

Several determined efforts were made during the day to take and re-take Dutch Folly. This island, almost within a stone's throw of the Bund, was in the hands of the Communists. Trenches

had been dug and from these, Commu ist marines opened fire at Yunnanese outposts and pickets on the Bund. After several mercenaries had been picked off, the Yunnanese burst open the doors of the Tai Sam Yuen restaurant as its roof is the highest in the vicinity. Previous to this, the staff had locked and barricaded the doors and fled. Finding a vantage point on the restaurant roof which had battlements of a kid, the mercenaries took cover and sent over volley after volley with their mausers. Finding their position untenable, the marines withdrew. Some fled in waiting while others jumped into the river, with full equipment in sheer fright.

I was privileged to watch the return action from a roof forty feet away. The Communists re-conustered and stole back on to the Island from the far side. They opened fire once more and caught mercenaries unaware. The latter returned to their unfailing roof, almost out of the range of the fire from the marines and banged away till the marines retreated once more. SOUTH FOLLOWING EVENTS: CLOSELY

When I left, the Island was, apparently, vacant, neither side venturing to take possession as it has no means of retreat. The marines were by no means accurate in their shooting although they did smash a considerable part of the restaurant's front. Some of their shots went wider than where I was a spectator.

When the river streamers arrived this morning, the Paul Beau was leading and it dropped anchor in the stream. The Sai On went ahead to her wharf and the Kinshan followed suit. The Honam was already anchored in the river. As far as I could see, none of the shot were directed at the boats and the mercenaries on the Bund were particularly anxious to avoid hitting the steamers.

At the moment of writing, firing seems to have slackened.

headline: $250,000 Bribe?
text: Canton, Saturday 4:30 p.m. Fighting broke out a short while ago through the River defence Flotilla steaming up the Canton River in line and opening an aimless bombardment. Shooting Affray.

Yangtzepoo district was the scene of Wednesday's shooting affray, which resulted in the death of two rioters and the wounding of several more. The disturbance occurred at a Japanese ice factory on Lay Road, within a few minutes walk of the Yangtzepoo Police Station. A crowd of about 3,000 assembled at the gates of the factory, forced their way in-side and for the next few minutes set about smashing up everything breakable. Matters became very serious and the Sikh constable on duty nearby summoned assistance which came from a squad of foreign and Chinese Police. The mob turned its attention to the Police who were forced to fire. One of the rioters was killed instantly while several suffered minor wounds. Later a hand to hand struggle took place between the police and the crowd and one of the most troublesome rioters received a blow on the head from a police baton which killed him.

headline: POSSIBLE
text:
ANOTHER SUGGESTION.

Sir Charles Eliot To Return to the Colony?

With the near approach of His Excellency the Governor's departure from Hongkong rumour is busier than ever with the intriguing subject of his successor.

A “China Mail” correspondent writes pointing out that a recent cable referred to the appointment of a new Ambassador at Tokyo without specifying the nature of the future activities of the Rt. Hon. Sir Charles Eliot, who has acted as British Ambassador to Japan since 1919. Would it be too great a flight of the imagination, he asks, to infer that the Home Government has him in view as the future Governor of Hongkong?

Of Sir Charles' eminent suitability for the post there can be no two ways of thinking. As the first Vice-Chancellor of the University of Hongkong, which post he held for many

years, he had peculiar opportunities of studying Oriental psychology, and the long list of important posts he has held speaks volumes as to his administrative and diplomatic ability. Amongst them are the High Commissionership of Samoa and British East Africa, also that of Commander-in-Chief of the latter Protectorate and H.M.'s High Commissionership in Siberia. Besides these he has held numerous posts in connection with the Embassy in the Near East and the United States of America.

The only arguments which rise to the mind in connection with such an appointment are those concerned with the nature of the political opinions of Sir Charles, which are not exactly coincident with those of the Party in power; also Sir Charles Eliot's age, which is just over 60: "Are these sufficient to over-ride the many and stronger arguments in favour of his appointment as Governor to Hongkong?" asks our correspondent, and dealing with the latter question the writer recalls Sir Charles Eliot's robust physique and Keen mental faculties which, he states, "so far from diminishing as the years' roll by seem ever to leave him with a clearer vision and a greater mastery in the direction of his faculties to the desired end." “It is fairly obvious,” writes our correspondent. “that it is not the intention of the Government to appoint a new Governor to administrative during what is undoubtedly the most trying period of the year. Again indulging the imaginative element, excusable enough in view of the suitability of Sir Charles, what more desirable than that he should have a few months' holiday when his post is filled in Japan and that he should then return to the Colony in connection with which he has held an important post with much distinction.”

headline: AMERICAN RESIDENT CHARGED.
text:
ALLEGED RFCKLESS DRIVING.

INDIAN CONSTABLE BADLY INJURED.

Before Mr. S. B. B. McElberry, at the Central Magistracy this morning, a young American named H. T. Werschkul, was charged on four counts arising out of a motor accident at Repulse Bay Road last Saturday afternoon. The charges were that he did (1) unlawfully drive a motor car without a proper licence, (2) drive while in an intoxicated condition, (3) fail to stop after causing injuries to an Indian guard of the Repulse Bay Hotel, and (4) drive recklessly. A formal adjournment was made

A formal adjournment was made for one week; bail being fixed at $2,000.

Mr. M. H. Turner appeared for the defence.

The accident happened near the Repulse Bay Hotel, and it is alleged that the car did not stop until it reached Shaukiwan Road where Divisional Inspector Blackman was on the lookout after a telephone message had been sent to the Police station there. The car was lying on the compound of the Central Police Station this morning. The glass of the right headlight was smashed and the number plate was defted. The Indian, although not in danger of his life, sustained a serious fracture of the hip which is likely to keep him in hospital for a long time.

text: Mounted police rode into a crowd of 10,000 persons who stormed the doors of Madison Square Garden, New York, into which 15,000 others had already fought their way to hear Eugene Debs, former radical prisoner and defeated Socialist candidate for President, who spoke at the behest of the Working's Circle National Convention. headline: SEARCH INCIDENT. / A P.W.D. EMPLOYEE IN TROUBLE.
text:
A Chinese draughtsman of the P.W.D., was charged before Mr. E.W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning with refusing to be searched at King Lane at 9.30 last night.

A Wei-hai-wei constable stated in evidence that he stopped the defendant as he wanted "to search him. The defendant asked what right witness had to search him, and witness pointed to his khaki uniform and revolver. Defendant refused to submit and had to be arrested.

The defendant stated that the constable approached him and felt him up and down when he (defendant) caught hold of the constable's hands and questioned his authority, whereupon, the constable assaulted him and arrested him.

His Worship was unable to accept the evidence of one man against another and discharged the defendant with a caution, saying that he would report the matter to the head of the P.W.D

headline: BRÚTAL MURDER / BODY THROWN INTO THE SEA.
text:
The partly decomposed body of a Chinese was found washed ashore on a beach in the mainland during the week-end in circumstances pointing to the man having been brutally murdered. The right side of the face bore a hole apparently caused by a bullet, and there were several stab wounds on the body. A piece of rope hanging from the girdle points to the theory that a stone weight was used to sink the body in the sea.

headline: WHOLE PROVINCE BEING INVOLVED.
text:
INCREASED FIRING

Increased firing which is thought to presage a big battle in a day or two is the principal feature of latest reports from Canton.

Once more the interruption to telegraphic communication is hindering the gathering of news. However, if there had been any sonsational development, the Naval authorities would have certainly been informed by wireless. Our Canton correspondent writes up to the hour of the mail closing yesterday afternoon. The Senior Officer of the West River reported also yesterday afternoon, by wireless, that there had been little change but that snipping was on the increase.

headline: NEW STOCK OF
text:
" Large crowds have been down to the water-front watching the Canton steamers arrive with full loads of refugees. There has been no recurrence of trouble, but the police have men out to look after the recruits arriving from Haiphong for the Yunnanese. Some of these have been unfavourably received, while a waiting transhipment to Canton have been threatened by the coolie classes. Their number will little effect the trend of events. "

Many refugees continue to arrive. A large number would like to leave Honam but cannot cross the river as the ferries have ceased to run.

headline: Shots at Ships.
text:
Canton night boats returning to Hongkong this morning report having been fired on from the shore early yesterday morning in the neighbourhood of the village of Chung Chow, Collinson Reach, (not, of course, to be confused with Cheung Chau near Hongkong).

The shots were rifle shots and one report attributes them to bands of outlaws (still wearing the soldiers' uniform of the army from which they have deserted for their own purposes) who were noticed at the spot the previous day. The locality in question is Danés Island, part of the larger Whampou group. Collinson Reach is not usually used by the boats but this has been necessary since the outbreak of hostilities because of the position the gun-boats have taken up at Canton. The Ko Chow (Captain Eb. Jones) was the first boat to pass the spot. She was keeping close to the shore and the shots were fired from almost point-blank range, loud demands being made at the same time for the ship to stop. Captain Jones, however, ordered full steam ahead and got clear of land without apparently any harm being done to passengers or ship. A Chinese patrol launch which at that moment came down the river proceeded to the spot where the firing had come from and fired four shots from its guns.

Towards yesterday evening, cross-river firing decreased and last night was somewhat quieter. This development is considered to be the usual lull before the storm. Hourly, the campaign is becoming more intricate and an initial success would do much to bring in the waverers in on the victors' side. Particulars have been obtained

of the casualties caused by the bombardment on Saturday afternoon and in the city during the sniping from Honam. Altogether there have been a dozen or so Chinese non-combatants killed in the various parts of the city and on the Bund. The round that fell in the Public Park has left a big cavity there.

The Red Navy is still more or less inactive although their guns are trained on Canton and all the vessels have steam up.

There have been no more struggles for Dutch Folly which is now vacant and untenable by either side.

A fair amount of damage has been done to buildings on and near the Bund.

Shameen's Safety.

To-day the river steamers are not going alongside their wharves as these have been declared to be in the war zone. They are at anchor in the stream off Shameen.

All the foreign gunboats—three British, two American, two French and one Japanese—are standing by.

Allies of the Cantonese Communists are coming down the West River. Their artillery has been finding its mark and shots have passed over Shameen which is still immune from immediate danger.

headline: HUGE AIRSHIP NOSES ABOUT IN.FOG FOR MOORING MAST.
text: A Reuter cable from Washington to-dny reports that the alrship "Los Angeles" was compolled to abandon a flight owing to engine trouble and could not find her mooring mast on account of fog. Our photograph shows the "Los Angeles."

headline: Firing Increases.
text:
After the lull of last night, the Yunnanese have been renewing and increasing their sniping at Honam and the Cantonese on that side have replied hotly. I am informed that the Yunnanese will try to keep up a barrage till they can effect a landing in the Red St-onghold, but without artillery it will be very difficult for them to do so. Although the firing has increased, the effect has decreased as both sides are taking good cover behind their sandbags and barricades.

headline: Shanghai; June 9.
text:
Three hundred Chinese seamen on six Butterfield & Swire coastal and river steamers at Shanghai went on strike yesterday evening. Ocean-going steamers are not affected.

Japanese lines are also meeting difficulties and are considering replacing the Chinese crews with Japanese.

Jardine, Matheson & Co. report unrest but no actual crew strike. A Jerdine coaster sailed yesterday night.

The strike of the dockers has interrupted dock work. Very little cargo is moving because the Chinese banks and shipping hongs which finance and handle cargo are closed down.

headline: 3,000 MORE.
text:
MINOR INGIDENTS

SHOTS FIRED OVER INSPECTOR'

Three thousand workers employed by Messi Butterfield and Swire struck today at Pootung. They were mostly casual workers.

There have been a number of minor incidents such as mud-throwing at American naval men at the border bridge.

The Chinese police were with difficulty persuaded to interfere.

The Chinese merchant volunteers actually fired shots over the head of Inspector Beale while the latter was on horseback on the Municipal Road.

The Eastern Extension Telegraph Co. notifies that the delay on telegrams for Shanghai and beyond has now been removed.

headline: A Bishop's Views.
text:
The Bishop of St. Albans, speaking at the Diocesan conference, said they must not lay all the blame for the disturbances in China on Bolshevism. They are largely due to the appalling conditions prevailing in industries in China and the fact that many Europeans have sought to make money from China without considering the native.

The conference passed a resolution declaring that greater sacrifices must be made by the Church at Home in order to further foreign missionary effort.

The question of the Shanghai shooting incidents was raised at a meeting of the workers' delegates of the International Labour Conference in a statement signed by Mr. Joshi (India); Mr. Lawson (Australia) and Mr. Suzuki (Japan) submitted to the Chairman.

The latter declared the question could not be raised in conference under standing orders, whereupon the meeting resolved to despatch through the Amsterdam International a message of sympathy to the workers of China.

headline: Strikers' Demands.
text:
Various Chinese Commercial and Student Unions met in the Chinese Chamber of Commerce last evening. They passed seventeen resolutions, which were handed to the Chinese delegates. They include four demands, which the strikers consider essential as preliminaries to official negotiations.

They are:—(1) The cancellation of a state of emergency; (2) the withdrawal of the marines; (3) the release of the arrested rioters; and (4) the restoration of closed schools.

Apologies Sought. Other resolutions reveal wide aspirations, including, the early cancellation of extraterritoriality; that the British and Japanese Ministers meanwhile should apologise to the Chinese Government and guarantee no further similar action; the abolition of the Mixed Court; the appointment of high Chinese officers to the Municipal Police; Chinese representation on the Shanghai Municipal Council in accordance with the amounts paid in taxes; payment of damages to the dependants of those killed or injured in the strike; payment of business losses

Approached this morning and asked how the system was working, Dr. Addison said that it was proving of the greatest possible use. At present nothing but the report of the nature of the disease and the number of deaths (or the recording of a clean bill of health is the case might be) was sent, but it was hoped that when the system was more firmly established, ed reports would be made of the nature of the steps taken to combat the disease and the measure of success which had attended them.

The number of ports making use of the Bureau was continually growing and his weekly cable from Singapore now included statistics from ports in Australia, said Dr. Addison. He himself sent off a cable to Singapore once a week telling them what was happening, and this was despatched by Singapore to all the ports who were partier to the scheme.

The advantages of the Bureau were that steps could be taken to deal with ships from infected ports arriving in Hongkong very much more quickly and with consequently more favourable results than when the news merely "filtered through" as Dr. Addison put it. He was confident that the result of the new system would be that the movement of infectious disease would be much more effectively restricted and when the system expanded and it was made possible to follow the result of the putting into practice of latest scientific discoveries he was confident that this would constitute an even greater step forward.

The Bureau was being made use of, said the P.C.M.O., by ports in Japan, Shanghai, French Indo-China, Siam, the Philippines, Dutch East Indies, Borneo, Australia, Singapore, Penang and British India, in fact practically over India.

It is interesting to recall that this matter of the incidence of epidemic diseases formed the subject of debate at the Medical Conference recently held at Hongkong and Dr. Lim, one of the first students to graduate from the Hongkong University, who has since interested himself in matters of health primarily in relation to Shanghai, had some interesting comments to make.

Dr. Lim pointed out that in these days of rapid communication and means of communication the control of infectious diseases, instead of being a matter of purely local significance, had become a subject of international concern. Improved means of communication had resulted in bringing cities and nations into closer touch, but this had not been without its attendant evils, as it had introduced diseases into territories where they had been non-existent. The fight would have to be waged on a worldwide basis if there was to be success, said Dr. Lim.

headline: HEALTH FIRST.
text:
BUREAU'S GOOD WORK.

Why Hongkong Is One of the "Plums."

Not the least important of the measures which, in Mrs Austen Chamberlain's words will make Hongkong still further one of the "plans" of the Colonial Service is the recently established health Bureau, the working of which was described to a "China Mail" representative this morning by the B.C.M.O.

Dr. J. B. Addison represented the Coloy at the conference held at Singapore, two months ago as a result of which the Epidemiological Intelligence Bureau was established for the purpose of collecting and disseminating information regarding the health conditions at the principal reports of the Far East.

On his arrival back in Hong Kong he told a "China Mail" representative that he was to act as the disseminator and collector for Hongkong and that he would receive news each week from other ports as to exactly what was happening there in regard to

and also the non-passage of a number of proposed Municipal and trade regulations.

headline: Marines Landed.
text:
Two hundred marines from H.I.J.M.S. Tatsuta landed this morning.

Two Japanese gun-boats from the Yangtze have left for Shanghai. Four Japanese destroyers have arrived, two of which have gone up river to protect foreigners at Yangtze ports.

The student demonstration at Foochow was a fiasco, owing to the Tupan's precautionary measures.

Chinkiang, Tsingtao, Kiukiang and Hankow are now quiet. While there have been no disturbances at Shanghai, the strike situation is unchanged. Defence measures are continuing. Further arrivals of naval men have enabled the authorities to lighten the duties of the volunteers.

Diplomatic Investigation.

Reports from Nanking indicate that the situation there is becoming more serious.

A telegram from Taiyuanfustates that rioter's wrecked the local agency of the Asiatic Petroleum Company, smashing windows and tearing down the sign. It is understood that Chang Tso-lin contemplates issuing a circular telegram advising the students to refrain from acts of violence pending diplomatic investigation.

Members of the diplomatic delegation left for Shanghai this morning by the "blue express." It is stated that they will not sit as a commission nor take formal evidence, but make independent investigations returning within a few days with their report.

The directors of the local Chinese Bankers' Association this morning decided: Firstly, to telegraph to the Chinese banks at Shanghai urging them to support the students; secondly, to telegraph to public bodies urging them to pursue the present agitation to the end; thirdly, to furnish $10,000 strike relief funds; fourthly, to advise native banks to refrain from co-operating financially with the foreign banks concerned.

The students here have gone out on a sympathetic strike. There is growing intensity against foreigners and the situation is most serious.

headline: MORE TROUBLE.
text:
KIUKIANG COOLIES STRIKE.

A telegram from Klukiang says that all the coolies struck work to-day.

The agent of the Indo-China Steam Navigation Company does not recommend passengers to proceed to Kuling.

A Chinese received injuries to his head in a motor accident at Queen's Road Central yesterday, the motor car did not stop and so far has not been traced.

headline: HOME POLICY.
text:
Support for the British officials on the spot is the keynote of the Home Government's policy as regards the trouble in Shanghai.

Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co.'s crews struck at nine o'clock yesterday evening and their steamers are laid up at the wharves.

Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co. propose concerted action by the big shipping companies.

The Nippon Kisen Kaisha boats have up to the present adhered to schedule.

The Fengyang Maru left Shanghai for Hankow this morning carrying passengers but no cargo, the former including representatives of the Chinese Associations known to be going to Nanking and Chinkiang with the object of disaffecting the crews of foreign steamers at those ports. Further: Nippon Kisen Kaisha

Further Nippon Kisen Kaisha sailings are unlikely.

A student demonstration and general strike took place to-day. The situation is quiet, but it is strained.

Trooper Attacked. (Shanghai Mercury) SHANGHAI. Jure 5 Tough no. Very serious, a number of incidents took place to-day to remind the authorities of

the acute situation with which they are faced and served to keep alive the fact that hostility has by no means abated.

The most serious incident today was an ambush attack in the early part of the forenoon upon Trooper Beale of the Bubbling Well Police Station. Trooper Beale was patrolling the Jessfield Brennan Road district and was about to cross the junction of these two roads when reports of guns rang out and three or four bullets whizzed past the mounted police man who sprang from his pony, unslinging his rifle at the panic time.

Crouching behind the bank at the side of the road, the officer waited for further firing, and he re-mounted after a glance around and returned to report to the Bubbling Well Station. About half a dozen shots are believed to have been fired in all. This district is approximate to that patrolled by the Chinese Volunteers, who have been protesting against Municipal Police patrols of late.

In the House of Commons, reply-ing to questions by Mr. F. W.

Pethiek Lawrence (Labour) and the Rt. Hon. C. T. Trevelyan (Labour), with regard to the troubles in China, Mr. Ronald McNeill, Under Secretary of Foreign Affairs, emphasized that the international authorities on the spot were faced with a situation of imminent danger to life and property and could not wait to obtain instructions from their governments before taking the necessary steps to restore law and order. Mr. McNeill deeply regretted that the attack of the forces of disorder had been conducted behind a screen of misguided students, but said the British Consul General at Shanghai, with whom he understood the American, French, Italian and Japanese representatives were fully agreed, had reported that the police were very patient and could not have acted otherwise than they did. The British Government was confident the Chinese Government was anxious to co-operate with the other governments concerned in reaching an equitable and satisfactory solution of this deplorable affair.

headline: Order First.
text:
Mr. McNeill emphasised that law and order must be restored and maintained in the international settlement and the Government would give all necessary support to the British officials on the spot. Mr. McNeill expressed sympathy with the Chinese people and deep regret that lives had been lost as a result of a misguided agitation.

The policy of His Majesty's Government to China, whose traditions and civilisation we admired, and with whose national aspirations we sympathised, who was our ally in the war and with whom we, were united in close and long standing ties, was animated by the solo concern that China should become peaceful and prosperous. The British Government recognised the obligation to help China in this task and looked to the forthcoming tariff conference to provide an opportunity for doing so in cooperation with the other Powers.

Mennwhile he trusted nothing would be done to prejudice or post-poetic those hopes.

headline: Origin of the Trouble.
text: Replying to Mr. Trevelyan with regard to the origin of the trouble at Shanghai, Mr. McNeill said that the accounts were conflicting, but the policy of His Majesty's Government had long been to use its influence in China to ameliorate labour conditions. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, Leader of the Opposition, asked were the Government enquiring into the industrial origin of the trouble. Mr. McNeill said that they were inviting the fullest information with regard to the whole incident. headline: Russian Arrested.
text: Special Police attached to Louza Station at 11:30 this morning arrested a young Russian named Klopfer and placed him in custody at the Louza Station. Members of the Volunteer Corps on duty along Nanking Road had observed Klopfer loafing around "Fokien Road corner for a period of upwards of two hours and, considering his actions suspicious, informed the Specials on patrol and had him removed. Klopfer, who gave his residence as Broadway, stated that he was waiting for a fellow-countryman. He is being held for further inquiries.

headline: CARGO OF FLOUR.
text:
CONFISCATION CLAIM.

Before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry, at the Central Magistracy this morning, an application was made under the Merchandise Marks Ordinance by Mr. H. L. Dennis, representing Messrs. H. Skott and Company, flour merchants, for a confiscation order in respect of 800 bags of flour which were an infringement of the "Battleship" trade mark, the property of his clients. Samples of the infringed mark and the original were exhibited in Court, the former bearing identical marks with the exception that the Company's name was omitted. The flour had been seized in the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company's godown, consigned from Shaughal to various Chinese dealers, who claimed to be interested only as sellers on a commission basis.

In applying for confiscation of the cargo, Mr. Dennis said he would not suggest that the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company were in any way to blame as they only acted as shippers and redownkeepers. He asked His Worship to thereafter make an order for a certain proportion of the flour to be handed to his client, to reimburse them for the costs of the proceedings in the same way as was done in a case which came before Mr. R. E. Li disell in 1919. Mr. R. A. Wadeson, appearing for the shippers, said that his clients should be exonerated from blame, and he considered that they also should receive part of the cargo to meet godown charges and

other expenses. They were quite an innocent party. Mr. Dennis agreed.

His Worship considered that before an order could be made an endeavour should be made to trace the owners of the cargo. On Mr. Dennis undertaking to draft an advertisement, the case was adjourned since die.

Shunghải, June 10.

The Nippon Yusen Kaisha are shipping cargo in mid-stream at the Pootung side and also at the wayside wharf under the protection of a Japanese gunboat.
The Butterfield & Swire position is not changed. Ocean-going steamers are not affected except by the fact that the merchandise is dwindling. For instance, there is no tea leaving.

headline: CANTON FIGHTING. / OUTLOOK STILL VERY CRITICAL
text:
REDS FROM WEST.

The Yunnanese are strengthening their position in Canton but it seems as if engagements will have to be fought in other parts of the province before the present Canton campaign can be brought to a close.

Danger to Shameen? Little or no news came through this morning owing to the telegraph land-lines being interrupted. The Naval authorities report no material change in the situation.

Most starting of all is the report from the “China Mail” Canton correspondent that the Cantonese Reds hint that two Russian warships will be coming to their aid.

On Monday, the "China Mail" reported that it appeared as if the Red Navy at Canton had been "influenced" by Yunnance money. Conflicting reports have since come down. From the latest messages, it appears that the Red flagship, the obsolete cruiser Wing Fung, formerly of the First Northern Squadron and recently re-named the Chung San in honour of Dr. Sun Yat-sen, has gone over to the mercenaries, but the statement of her having bombarded her old colleagues in Honam has yet to be confirmed. On Monday it seemed as if those of the River Defence Flotilla which fired up the River and anchored off the Macao Forts, were trying to make for Whampoa to bring up reinforcements

Intermittent sniping continues but the Cantonese stronghold on Honam, across the River, appears as if it is being vacated. On the attitude of the Wing Fung (Captain Au Yeung) and the gunboats becoming suspicious, the Reds began to move away from the Cement Works. at Honam. To-day there have been very few casualties on the Canton side and the fire from Honam is weakening. General Leung Hung-kai has despatched an expedition of 3,000 men who are marching on Shek Wai Tong with the object of threatening Canton from the West. The Yunnanese scouts at Wongsha are very active and long range bombardment may be the order of things at any moment.

There are 10,000 or so Yunnanese and Kwangsi riflemen at Shektan with orders to hold up the Red advance at any cost. At the White Cloud Mountains are Yunnanese headquarters. As these heights overlook the eastern and northern approaches to Canton, they are very strongly fortified and General Yang Hsi-nan is directing operations there in person. Outside army headquarters are posted 40 machine-guns and about 20 light artillery pieces. The 2nd division is also on the heights under Commander Chu Wai. Lieut.-General Liu Hang-chiu is the defender of Canton. The western suburb (the main business centre) is very peaceful and the civil population is moving about unconcernedly.

Another aeroplane was up above the city this afternoon distributing leaflets warning the people to leave in six hours when a bombardment from the air would start.

General Chan Kwing-ming and Lin Fu are now reported to be active but it can be taken for granted that they will not join the fight till the issue is nearly decided.

Among the leaflets circulated in Canton are those purporting to originate from the following, all anti-Bolshevik: — Farmers, labourers and merchants, Yunnanese and Kwangsi mercenaries, the “elder” (i.e. conservative) members of the Kuomintang; and some military students.

Well-known Man Killed.

A shot from Honam richocheted and killed Mr. Wong; the proprietor of the Washington Café on the Bund. Mr. Wong, who is best-known as “Fatty,” was a Canton landmark.

I am informed that at the fight for Dutch Folly Island, 60 Yunnanese were opposed to about 100 Reds who had machine-guns. The latter threw their weapons into the River when they tried to swim away on meeting a searching fire from the restaurant roof. (Full details in Monday's "China Mail.")

Attack by Night?

Yunnanese headquarters state that had it not been for the “deflection” of the Communist Navy, the Cantonese on Honam would have planned a determined landing on the east of Canton, after the style of Gallipoli, under cover of a naval bombardment.

A few shells had previously been fired at Taishatau where there is a Yunnanese camp, apparently, to clear the place. With the failure of the small boats to bring up the Red "Cadets" from Whampoa and the disinterest of the flagship, this attack is not likely to eventuate. Otherwise Canton city, or at least the eastern part, might have experienced the first real battle of the campaign.
With the spread of the campaign, fighting, may take place close to Shameen.

Yesterday the Customs main building on the Bund was closed and business is now transacted from Shameen.

Two Bolsheviks are rumoured to have been expelled from Shameen on Saturday night.

headline: HANKOW TRAGEDY.
text:
RIOTERS ATTEMPT TO RUSH ARMOURY.

SUDDEN CRISIS.

Foreigners Compelled To

Owing to a state of extreme emergency suddenly arising, machine guns had to be used against rioters at Hankow yesterday.

headline: FALSE REPORTS.
text:
Hankow, June 11. Following false reports in this morning's vernacular papers, an anti-foreign riot took place this evening.

The volunteers were called out. The rioters rushed the Bund. They tore up seats and wrought destruction in Japanese shops. They severely mauled a Japanese shopkeeper.

Later the rioters broke down a barricade and attempted to rush the British volunteer armoury.

The rioters were in heavy numbers totally outnumbering the defence force of the armoury. The fire brigade ineffectually turned hoses on the mob after which, there being a state of extreme emergency, under orders of the Navy, the rioters were fired on with machine guns.

Eight were killed. The number of wounded is not yet known. At present all is quiet and the Chinese authorities guaranteed continued peace.

[Hankow, June 11.—Following a coolies' dispute last night at Messrs. Butterfield and Swire's upper wharf, in which a great deal of stone throwing took place, a squad of Chinese police fired over the crowd and scattered it. A dozen arrests were made. The trouble was apparently purely Chinese, but this morning when the upper wharf coolies attempted to resume work they were mobbed and prevented from doing so.

A strike was declared, the students haranguing the coolies.—Reuter.]

headline: China's Third Note.
text:
In spite of the official statement that the Note would not be made public till to"morrow, the Note that was handed in to Signor Cerruti, Italian Minister, this evening was handed out to the pressmen in French and Chinese at nine o'clock.

The Note takes cognisance of the fact that the Powers view the incident in the same conciliatory spirit as the Chinese Government and that instructions have been given to the police of the International Settlement to cease the use of arms.

The Note goes on to insist that the steps taken by the authorities of the Settlement to hinder a "pacific student demonstration" were badly devised and denies that there was the state of imminent danger to which the Powers' communication referred.

The Concession authorities and not the unarmed students are therefore responsible for the deplorable events. The Government, in view of the indignation prevailing to-day throughout the country, begs to give general advice to the Concession authorities which the latter should follow, namely to raise the state of siege, re-embark the marines, disarm the volunteers and police, free the arrested men, restore the occupied schools, for the restoration of order in Shanghai with the briefest possible delay.

The Note asks the Ministers to instruct their consular representatives accordingly.

headline: SHANGHAI TROUBLE. / SHEAF OF QUESTIONS IN COMMONS.
text:
OFFICIAL ATTITUDE.

China's Disorders the Root Cause of the Strike.

That the Home Government has a sound grasp of the Shanghai trouble is apparent from another official statement made in the House of Commons yesterday.

A number of questions lodged in the House of Commons regarding the Shanghai trouble, elicited long replies from Mr. Ronald McNeill, Under Secretary—of Foreign Affairs, who expressed the opinion that the trouble was mainly due to unsettled conditions owing to the lack of a strong central government, the destructive wars and the irritation of the Chinese with petty local rulers resulting in discontent which had been skillfully directed by interested parties

against the foreigners whose treaty rights they represent as inimical to the well-being of China.

Mr. McNeill added that for some time past the British Government had been giving close attention to the question whether industrial conditions were playing an appreciable part in the general widespread unrest in China.

Mr. McNeill expressed the opinion that such conditions were hardly operative at all as the cause of the present troubles, though any such discontent as far as it existed should be welcomed as the symptom of a desire for better things.

He pointed out that the strike began in a Japanese cotton mill where the conditions were equal or superior to anything in China.

Mr. McNeill declared that the British Government had long been exerting active pressure on the international authorities at Shanghai to secure improved factory conditions in the foreign settlement, especially as regards child labour with the aim of making the settlement a model for the rest of China. It now intends to seek a solution of the difficulties in a conciliatory spirit while insisting on the maintenance of law and order in the foreign settlement.

headline: STOP PRESS. / A MASS MEETING.
text:
A mass meeting of 25,000 students and workers was held at the recreation ground in the Shanghai Chinese city yesterday evening under the auspices of the Citizens Association. The participants wearing black arm bands made stirring speeches.

Resolutions were passed (1) to sever economic relations with the British and Japanese on June 12; (2) to urge the Central Government to secure satisfaction for the shooting on May 30 from the British and Japanese; and (3) failing settlement in a fortnight to declare at general strike throughout the country.

The meeting afterwards marched in procession to the native city. During the march two Japanese posing as Chinese students were violently handled and taken to a police station and locked up.

Special trains: conveyed the crowds to and from the native city and the Chapel suburb.

headline: SHANGHAI TROUBLES. / HOW GREATER BLOODSHED WAS AVERTED.
text:
FOMENTERS OF UNREST?

The British Co-operating With the Powers.

Had the mob in Shanghai seized the arms in the Police Station on May 30 there would have been greater bloodshed, declared Mr. A. M. Samuel in the House of Commons, when he pointed to the co-operation of the Powers and the surest remedy for the disturbances.

headline: LABOUR CONDITIONS.
text:
The position in China was the subject of a number of questions by Labour members and others in the House of Commons.

Replying to a suggestion by Mr. Will Thorn (Labour) that the trouble in Shanghai was due to low wages and the employment of children, Mr. A. M. Samuel, Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Overseas Trade, for the Foreign Office emphasised that the British Government had done all it could to improve conditions of labour within the International Settlement and had no control outside. The mob at Shanghai was very large and murderous. Had they succeeded and seized the arms at the police station there undoubtedly would have been greater bloodshed. The British policy in respect of the trouble in China had been adopted in concert with the other Powers interested and no points of difference had arisen. Mr. Samuel paid a tribute to the firm and tactful manner in which the Italian Minister, Signor Cerruli, the senior diplomat in Peking, was handling the situation. He (Mr. Samuel) emphasised that the Government respected China, and would gradually lend all support with a view to securing China's prosperity and peace. The casualties in Shanghai were 21 Chinese killed, 65 Chinese wounded, and one American wounded.

The Hankow Affair. The British Consul at Hankow reported that the firing there was inevitable. Had the Chinese authorities co-operated with the defence force, a deplorable loss of life would have been avoided.

The disturbances in Hankow and Shanghai were a symptom of the deep and widespread unrest exploited by interested parties to stir up feeling against those Powers with the largest interests in China who, therefore, were deeply concerned to co-operate with China in the task of progress and reform. The surest remedy for the anti-foreign feeling in China would lie in an attempt by the Treaty Powers to carry out the decisions of the Washington Conference in regard to co-operation between China and the Powers in measures beneficial to China. The Government was considering the best means of overcoming the difficulties arising largely from the absence of an effective Government in China. It trusted that the forthcoming conference on the internal Tariff of China would afford an opportunity of removing such obstacles, dissipating the present atmosphere of distrust and inaugurating an era of fruitful co-operation between China and the Powers.

An Important Point. Mr. Samuel emphasised that no Chinese were killed by British forces. The casualties were inflicted by the Police of the International Municipality of Shanghai.

Asked whether he would order that future demonstrators would not be fired on with ball cartridge, Mr. Samuel replied that the Government was not in a position to give instructions to an International Municipality. He added that the industrial conditions in the International Settlement in Shanghai were better than in the Chinese area over which we had no control.

headline: Optimistic View.
text:
Replying to Mr. Ramsay Mac-Donald Mr. Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister, gave the assurance that the Government was co-operating with the other Powers in taking every step possible to prevent the disturbances becoming a really big International trouble in the Far East. There was every reason to believe that the Powers and the Chinese

desire to attain peace, and enable an attempt to come to an arrangement on the Tariff which would keep and consolidate the Central Government of China.

headline: $45,000 IN DRUGS.
text:
SEQUEL IN COURT.

MARCHANT.

Before Mr. S. B. E. McElderry, at the Central Magistracy this morning, Matthew Tonkin, 37, native of England, and Moses Sansonovitch, 52, native of Brazil, both merchants, were formally charged with the unlawful importation of drugs into the Colony. The prosecution was a sequel to the discovery of a large quantity of heroin packed in tin tubes and concealed in the leg posts of a consignment of sixteen cases bed-steads consigned from Antwerp to Shanghai by the s.s. Glentani. The seizure was made by revenue

officers who found on a minute examination of the bedsteads that the legs were made to screw off.

Mr. H. A. Taylor, Assistant Superintendent of the Imports and Exports Office, informed His Worship that the actual amount of the seizure had not yet been ascertained, but it was about 150 lbs. of heroin. He asked for a few days' adjournment as he considered that it might be necessary to send a cable to the Colonial Office regarding the matter and probably await evidence from there. Mr. Taylor said that the evidence against the first accused was quite clear, but so far there was very little evidence against the second accused.

Mr. C. H. Lyson appeared for the defence.

The case was adjourned until noon on Friday, bail being fixed at $10,000 and $500 respectively. The value of the seizure amounts to about $15,000.

headline: WANTON MURDER. / SHANGHAI BRITON KILLED.
text:
WOMAN WOUNDED.

Terrible End to a Motor Car Drive.

Shanghai has been shocked by the brutal and wanton murder of a British resident whose fate was narrowly escaped by a lady who was with him at the time.

Miss Duncan, though wounded, took the steering wheel and guided the car more than a thousand yards, when it ran into a ditch near the Columbia Country Club, to which she ran.

In the course of a letter dated Shanghai, June 10, Mrs. Herbert Sutor writes to her father, Mr. D. McNeill, in Hongkong: “You are not getting many letters these days, but things have been so worrying and unsettled that we have not had time or heart to write. The Police did all they could do to quieten the mob, but it was useless. They drove the Police from Sincere's to Lonza Station, and then in the end the odds were so great that the Police had to fire. Fancy six men against a mad mob of 3,000.

“We could not get fresh meat for some days, but did quite well. The French told the shopkeepers that if they closed up they would lose their licences. They called off the boycott from the French Commission very quickly. Many—in fact, nearly all—have been left to do for ourselves, but we do not mind that.

"The Shanghai Scots have their headquarters in the Golf Club on the Racccourse, and the Americans have theirs in the New World. During the worst part of the trouble the Chinese were kept off the Nanking Road. It was just like a military town. But for a week we were at their mercy, the Chinese sniffing, throwing bricks, and sniping, whilst our poor boys were almost dronning with fatigue, after standing 36 hours!"

"Whilst it is certain that the Municipal Council will not stand any nonsense, it is felt that only international intervention can settle the trouble effectually."

headline: FATAL SHOTS.
text:
The Briton Mr. William Mackenzie was murdered last night while driving his car outside the Settlement boundaries with a lady, Miss Duncan, who was wounded. Seven Chinese stopped the car and turned flashlights on the occupants.

They fired at Mr. Mackenzie who had restarted the car. He was hit in the neck and fell forward.

headline: STOP PRESS. / PROTEST AND REPLY.
text:
The Commissioner for Foreign Affairs has protested to the British Consul regarding the firing on the mob. He says the firing was unnecessary and holds the Consul personally and the officer who ordered the firing, to be responsible therefor. He requests the withdrawal of the Naval contingent and that orders should given to refrain from firing in future.

The Consul replied yesterday evening that the protest was not reasonable and without foundation in fact. He corrects erroneous statements contained in the protest. He says that the firing was most necessary in view of the danger to foreign lives and property in the Concession, particularly following the serious damage already done by the rioters and the murder of a Japanese the same evening. He also states that fire was opened only as a last resort and even then was most restricted.

Fighting was audible yesterday afternoon to the North of Canton where, presumably the Cantonese are following up the remnants of the fleeing meccenary armies.

headline: SHANGHAI TROUBLE.
text:
STRIKE FUNDS LEVY.

Employees Who Must Give One Day's Pay a M

That the anti-foreign movement in China has the backing of the Peking Government is now established beyond doubt.

It is authoritatively learned that the Ministry of Communications has issued an order to the telegraph, postal and railway services that each employee will have one day's pay deducted a month as a contribution to the strike funds.

The street collections in aid of the Shanghai strikers have practically ceased.

text: The commission composed of the diplomatic representatives of the interested Powers' met this morning and issued a communique stating that if the Chinese Government so desired they would request authorisation from respective governments to discuss in the friendliest spirit the propositions presented, by their delegation at Shanghai with regard to the organisation of the International Settlement and the administration of justice therein.

headline: Shanghai Discussions. Shanghai, June 19.
text:
A statement by the Commissioner of Foreign Affairs this evening on behalf of the Chinese delegation asserts that Chinese opinion thought it necessary to include in the conference fundamental issues, such as rendition of the Mixed Court, amelioration of labour conditions, participation of Chinese on the Municipality which would not conflict with treaties but were legitimate aspirations of the Shanghai Chinese.

The points were presented to the Commission who evinced a desire to shift the responsibility of the events leading to the shooting to the Chinese authorities. The Diplomatic Commission stated that it had no authority to discuss international questions and has gone to Peking to report to the Ministers. The Chinese delegation regretted that so far sincere efforts for a peaceful solution had failed.

headline: Students Take Hint.
text:
As a result of the Consular Body's meeting with Tupan Hsiao Yao-nan yesterday afternoon, the Tupan has given a most exquisite assurance of protection for foreign lives and property with his 3,000 troops, following which the number of volunteers and blue-jackets is being reduced.

The Peking student agitators have returned to Peking, it is reported, following a hint from Hsiao Yao-nan.

Following a meeting of the diplomatic representatives of the interested Powers this morning, a communique was issued stating: The delegation of interested diplomatic representatives went to Shanghai solely on a mission of investigation. Later it had its powers enlarged and was brought into negotiation's with the Chinese delegates. The last named having presented demands which exceeded the powers of the delegation, the latter took note of the fact and is returning to make a report. The interested diplomatic representatives have already made known to the Wachiaopu their desire to begin negotiations without delay. In their opinion, immediate settlement of the Shanghai incidents themselves on a basis of justice and equity must be the object of a first agreement. Likewise if the Chinese Government expresses a desire the interested diplomatic representatives are disposed to request their respective Governments for authorisation to discuss in the friendliest spirit the propositions presented to their delegation in Shanghai concerning both the organisation of the International Settlement and the administration of justice therein.

headline: LOCAL STRIKE. / SEAMEN'S UNION'S DECISION.
text:
Steamiers

The Hongkong Seamen's Union has decided to take part in an anti-foreign strike “under orders from Canton.”

Out of a whole crop of rumours the most definite statement is that by Mr. Chan Kim-fook, secretary of the Hongkong Chinese Seamen's Union. He informed the "China Mail" that instructions were received from the parent labour union of China, at Canton, at nine o'clock this morning. The Hongkong Union was told to inform all Chinese seamen to cease work on foreign-owned steamers, river, coastal, or ocean-going. Chinese-owned shipping would be maintained to keep up communication. By this Mr. Chan meant that the boats owned by Chinese firms on the run between Hongkong and Canton would not be affected.

Broadly translated, Mr. Chan's reply to the "China Mail's" inquiry was: "In compliance with a general order from the General Labour Union of China, Canton,

against British, Japanese American goods. Anti-foreign outbreaks are feared. The Shameen authorities have taken steps to cope with all possible emergencies.

It is plainly evident that the Steamboat Co. vessels avoided going to Canton because it was felt that the crews would leave, or be made to leave, their ships there. Accordingly it may have been preferred to keep the ships here.

On inquiry at the Harbour Office it was learned that no shipping had been affected beyond the Steamboat Co.'s Canton vessels. Permits were still being taken out for coastal and ocean shipping this morning and cargo was being worked in all parts of the harbour. However, different conditions may prevail when the effect of Scamed's action is felt. Outside of the seamen, no other branch of workmen in Hongkong seem to have taken any action at a late hour this morning.
