headline: DANCERS KILLED.
text:
While a hundred persons, were participating in the Fourth of July celebrations at the Pickwick Club early in the morning and an orchestra was playing dance music, a wall of a five-storey building, weakened by adjacent excavations, crashed down on the dance floor, entrapping the dancers between the floor and the fallen metal ceiling work.

Rescue was most difficult, necessitating the removal of the front wall which threatened to collapse in addition to the debris. Hitherto twelve dead were brought out after a night and daylong search. Voices, chiefly of women, were heard calling for help from the debris early in the morning but became silent later.

headline: FALSE REPORTS.
text:
The American Chamber of Commerce has written to the Chinese Chamber of Commerce to endeavour to make known to the Chinese the true facts of the Hankow affair.

After warning the Chinese Chamber of the danger of allowing false reports—the American note says that there is nothing to add to the despatches from the Consuls to the Chinese authorities on June 15, which contained a complete and irrefutable statement on the Hankow incident, and encloses copies.

Attention is drawn to efforts being made to throw the full responsibility for the incident on the British authorities and the note says: it so happened that a point in the British Concession was attacked, but as the British Naval officer in charge of that post acted for the International community of Hankow, we, as part of the combined defence force which included French, Italians, Japanese and Americans, as well as British, must therefore accept our share of the responsibility of their action.

"We stand by them wholeheartedly, and urge you in fairness to co-operate in making this fact clear to the Chinese people."

headline: HENLEY REGATTA.
text:
Dull weather prevailed at Henley to-day, but a large 'crowd witnessed the finals in the various events. In the final for the Visitors' Cup, Third Trinity College (Cambridge) beat Brasenose (Oxford) by two lengths in 7 minutes 45 seconds. In the Grand Challenge Cup, Leander beat the Thames Rowing Club by three quarters of a length in 6 minutes 53 seconds, which is a record for the course.

In the Diamond Sculls, Beresford beat Gollan easily in 8 minutes 28 seconds.

Beresford interviewed after the racing said that he had relinquished the Philadelphia Gold Cup which he had handed back to the American oarsman Hoover.

His ground for doing this was that the English Amateur Rowing Association insisted that the Diamond Sculls constituted the World's Amateur Championship, and not the Philadelphia Cup as claimed by the Americans.

headline: RIFFI ATTACKS.
text:
FRENCH' REPULSE NIGHT OFFENSIVE

SHARP ENGAGEMENT.

A message from Fez states that violent Riff attacks were made on the night of July 5 on a group of French positions at Upper Leben, near Ainnatouf, and were repulsed with heavy losses. The French advanced north-west of Kiffane after a sharp engagement in which arms and munitions were captured. In view of the recent enemy infiltrations, women and children have, as a precaution, left Taza.

headline: DOSSER'S TRIAL.
text:
The evidence in the Dosser case was continued this morning. Two Russians, Detective Bebenim and Constable Kedrolizansky, who accompanied a British detective to arrest the accused couple, described the finding of incriminating documents, with especial regard "to a certificate from the Soviet Agitation Department.

Cross-examined, Bebenim admitted that he once worked for the Bolsheviks at Vladivostock, but denied that when sent on a Soviet mission from Vladivostock, he embezzled Soviet funds. He, however, admitted being sent on such a mission.

Kedrolizansky admitted that before joining the Municipal Police in Shanghai he was an officer in the White Russian Army at Vladivostok, also that he was formerly a political enemy of the Bolsheviks, who imprisoned him at Vladivostok. He was only released when the Japanese took over the port.

The case was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: EUROPEAN CHARGED.
text:
ALLEGED BREACH OF TRUST.

In the District Court at Singapore a European, named Mr. W. W. Matthews, was charged with criminal breach of trust in respect of $2,000 worth of watches belonging to Messrs. V. R. Vick and Co. Chief Court Inspector Meredith asked for a postponement for further investigations, as the accused was only just arrested.

The accused, who pleaded, not guilty, objected to a postponement, stating that if there was a case against him it was a civil case. He added that he was not an agent, but a partner with Mr. Vick, and that about $4,000 must be due to him from Mr. Vick.

Mr. Franklyn Robinson adjourned the case for a week, fixing bail at $2,000.

Shanghai, July 5.—Mr. MacMurray, the newly-appointed U.S. Minister to China, left Shanghai this afternoon on an American gunboat. He is expected to arrive in Tientain to-morrow afternoon. Reuter.

Washington. July 6.—Reports hitherto received by the War Department indicate that the test muster for defence forces yesterday was only two thirds as great as in September. Nevertheless the results are considered satisfactory.—Reuter's American Service.

Paris, July 8.—That protracted Franco-German commercial negotiations have broken down is attributed to the fact that both countries are about to introduce new Protectionist tariffs and that it is impossible to conclude a permanent convention until these are passed by Parliament.—Reuter.

headline: $3 a Day.
text: The statements made in "the course of the prosecution of a Kowloon house coolie yesterday do not give rise to satisfactory thoughts. General conversation has been devoted to the action of servants generally and the treatment to be meted when they returned. Yesterday's case proved that the servants of a prominent Kowloon resident lost no time in leaving his employment and later that he found the lowliest of them in other employment at $3'a day. Such a condition of things seems hopeless, suggests selfishness, and must tend to sour those who are seeking the good of the community by a uniform standard of settlement. Mr. Wylie has done good in taking the trouble to appear in court. It reveals the attitude of certain members of the community who have "money to burn" and also the fact that intimidation does not seem to count where emergency wages can be obtained by a coolie at the princely rate of $3 a day. Something drastic should be devised to meet such a state of affairs.

headline: BEHIND THE SCENES IN SHANGHAI.
text:
With uniform alacrity, press accounts of the serious anti-foreign movement in Shanghai and other Chinese cities have laid the blame at the gate of the Kremlin, says a "Christian Science Monitor" writer. In the news stories of a single day, in fact, one finds the "Rods" held responsible for French difficulties in North Africa; British difficulties in Afghanistan; and this Chinese outbreak in Shanghai. Unquestionably the potency of Moscow's influence has been widely-overestimated; and Communian, too often has been advanced to explain situations for which no other explanation could be found or for which a more accurate explanation was not held to be altogether desirable.

But with all due allowance for the exaggerated menace of Soviet propaganda—activities,—it—still remains most likely that Russian influence in China is the immediate cause of the present difficulty. When Karakhan, the present Soviet Ambassador, came to Peking he brought with him a staff, the size of which was more than passingly significant. The Ambassador, himself, did nothing to conceal his determination to reveal to the Chinese, on the one hand, "the treachery" of the powers in China, and, on the other hand, "the honesty" of the purposes of the Soviets.

As proof of this latter point the Soviets relinquished extra-territorial rights in China and made other promises—most of which have not fully been carried out. The relinquisition of extra-territoriality, however, proved to be a potent argument with the young Chinese and the Soviet representatives soon made a large place for themselves in certain of the intellectual circles of China.

The significance of this achievement cannot be over-estimated. In China the intelligentsia possess a status higher than accorded to them in Western nations. Many, perhaps most, of the great reform movements in China's history have been instigated by the student classes. The most recent example of this is found in the student uprising against Japan in 1919 which resulted in a nation-wide boycott of Japanese goods in protest against the award to Japan of rights in Shantung Province. The Soviets, having won the friendship of certain elements among the students, have allied with themselves one of the most powerful groups in the country. Having thus satisfied large numbers of these students that their purposes were honest, the Soviets proceeded to demonstrate the dishonesty of the Powers in their dealings with China. The hostility that resulted from this effort was apparent before the recent outbreak developed. This hostility took the form of an active anti-Christian movement. The headquarters of this movement were in Shanghai. The ones were established through

outside of them. In Foochow, in Fukien Province, for example, the Anglo-Chinese college was practically forced to close its doors recently because of the reign of terror inaugurated against Christians by a guerrilla student organization known as the "Blood and Iron Band."

It is this developing hostility that has now centered in Shanghai. The exact occasion for the trouble leaves something to be desired, from the point of view of the foreigners in the city. Industrial conditions in the foreign-owned mills of Shanghai are notoriously bad. A strike occurred recently in one of these mills, owned by a Japanese concern. The strikers were arrested, just why has not appeared. They were brought before the Mixed Court—a tribunal composed of a Chinese and a foreign justice to deal with cases affecting the interests of both Chinese and foreigners. The court jailed the strikers—This action—an action which sorely needs explanation—fanned the smouldering fires of re-sentment against foreigners. Students rushed in to infuiliate the labourers. Industry has practically closed down and a virtual state of war exists in the city.

That the Soviets, through their hold on student groups, are utilizing the situation to their own ends is undeniable. Communism thrives where there is trouble. Peace is contrary to the Soviet programme. Every incipient outbreak is hailed in Moscow with great glee, as hemiding the progress of world revolution.

Progress and justice, save in terms of violence and destruction, is invariably regarded with scorn by Moscow's trouble-brewers. That China has not always fared well at the hands of foreigners is undeniable. That progress toward better treatment is being made is equally undeniable. It is unquestionably the Soviet fear that this progress threatens their own programme taint had led them to foster, on whatever pretext presents itself, this anti-foreign uprising in China. A further fact needs to be kept in mind in regard to this difficulty. Neither all—or a majority—of the intelligent Chinese leaders or students are in sympathy with the Communist Party. There may be some basis for dissatisfaction with the decision of the Mixed Court. But reports coming from mission schools in China indicate that a vast number of the students have been awayed by Soviet propaganda and desire nothing more than peace for their country. Let like manner, the roll orders of Chinese life a great many of whom have studied in America and England will not be easily swung from a belief in orderly progress in violence.

Mr. Holyoak reminds us—and reminds us from his own vital experience—have been loyal and proved their loyalty in different directions, all of a practical nature. This section of the community deserves all that has been said of it. It has had to surmount. those inborn feelings of sympathy which come naturally, if unreasonably, when the actions of our nationals are the subject of discussion or rebuke. The national life is akin to the family life. Attack the one, and the members of it fall into either a defensive or offensive line. It is more than likely that in throwing in their lot with the British for either business or sentimental reasons, those who have earned for themselves the right to receive Mr. Holyoak's commendation, retain decided opinions as to the claims of China to be heard on such questions as extr-territoriality, Concessions, etc.; and the desire to have happenings at Shanghai and Shameen probed by an impartial board. If they do not, we shall be inclined to throw doubts on their possession of any sense of loyalty to anyone, and to say that they are merely of that class of opportunities which, of the Machiavellian, are the most Machiavellian. But those who have set themselves the task of assisting in the fostering of trade; the return of the workers, and a desire for right feelings as between foreigners and Chinese, give us confidence that British administration, justice, freedom, education, etc., have not been in vain, and that the fruits of these things are to be seen in this desire of a large and influential body of Chinese to recreate confidence and to set in motion again the wheels of finance and commerce. The two

Their position is no sinecure, and especially so at the present moment when doing good by stealth and without the flourish of trumpets is part of their daily work. Of the work of Dr. S. W. headline: Peculiar Morality.
text: A short-sighted attitude was that confessed to by a Chinese merchant in an interview yesterday on the question of supplying Canton with rice. He realised, he said, that the principles on which the. Canton Government was administering were opposed to the interests of the merchants, and thus it followed that he realised that the longer such Government continued the more complete would be the disastrous economic effects to himself. He had rice at Bangkok in connection with which he had incurred considerable liability, and he knew that there would be a market for it at Canton; although, as rice appears to be considerably cheaper than has been thought, his profit on the transaction will be comparatively small. What does he do? Think of the future, and, in the knowledge that on the cost of living will depend to a large extent the tenure of the Government do what he can to shorten that tenure? Not a bit of it. In the hope of cutting as much of his immediate loss as possible he decides to get rid of his rice in Canton at what price it will fetch, knowing full well that he will have to pay $1,000 for landing his cargo to the very Government whose existence he deplores and which is doing its best to strangle his interests. One can imagine his astonishment if he were told that his action might be liable to be construed as on a par with supplying the Canton Government with munitions of war. The sooner that he and others realise this the better it may be for their own interests.

headline: MOTOR CRASH.
text:
MAN WHO WOULD NOT BE WARNED.

An overturned bus on the road-side ought to have proved an effective deterrent as regards speed to a Chinese car driver who passed the scene whilst efforts were being made to extricate the vehicle. But according to evidence given before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday the driver seemed determined to emulate the example of his unfortunate colleague who had deposited the bus in the paddy field and as a result, a quarter of a mile further on, his vehicle also left the road and overturned.

The scene of the accident was the Cheung Shu Wan road and Sanitary Inspector Kerrison testified to the speed of the car being 45 to 50 miles an hour when it passed him shortly before overturning. The driver drove at a speed of 30 miles an hour over the chain blocks which were in the road in connection with the salvaging of the overturned 'bus' said Mr. W. R. Wong, of the Kowloon 'Bus Company'. Witness called to the driver, as he approached, to be careful of the blocks, but he took no notice and as he passed over the blocks a piece of iron which afterwards turned out to be the brake rod flew from the car nearly hitting the Manager. The driver in answer to the charge said he was not driving dangerously and the reason for the car leaving the road was that he had tried to avoid two small boys who ran across the road. headline: STRIKE BREAKERS.
text:
The stream runs dry, or, in other words, health, comforts, and advantages are seldom fully appreciated until they are lost. At the present moment too many of Hongkong's residents are aware of this truism, and to give instances would be both superfluous and irritating. However, bad though conditions have been for the past six weeks, a little consolation may be gained by the reflection that things might have been worse, Happily there has been no rationing of food, and for this fortunate state of affairs we owe a deep debt of gratitude to the Dairy Farm Company. Lack of space forbids us to go into details about the great amount of extra work being done by the depleted staffs at all the branches and in all departments of that essential organisation, so we shall merely give a few facts about their main shop at the top of Wyndham Street. From enquiries made a "China Mail" man learned that about thirty-five of the forty-two Chinese employees there walked out six weeks ago. Five of the faithful six were in the shipping department, and there they have remained during the strike. The other thirty-five clerks, butchers, sausage-makers, tripe-cleaners, picklers, pie-makers, bacon-curers, and coolies—downed tools and disappeared at the nod of the "dare to dies." To add to the troubles and worries of the few European employees the closing of the markets sent hordes of Chinese and others, who do not at other times patronise the place, up to the "Ngao Nei Xung Si." On the first day of the strike a Portuguese lady who, we understand, assisted there during the 1922 strike, took up her former position at the cash desk. She has been there every day since from 10 a.m. During the early morning spell, 7 a.m.—9 a.m., a Jewish gentleman and his wife act as cashiers. On the second day of the strike two well-known Queen's College masters walked into the shop and offered their services....They were received with open arms by the frantic staff and given jobs straight away, and every day for the past six weeks they have been at their posts from 7 a.m. till after closing time. Later on another master from the same school came to help. Further assistance has been rendered by several young ladies from the Italian Convent who come in relays of two at a time. Behind the scenes two mariners, a hefty soldier, and a Filipino, "Samson," have been doing a lot of heavy work. So little time have the regular employees and voluntary male assistants to spare that breakfast and tiffin are "bolted" on the premises. For the first three weeks of the strike the three butchers, Messrs. Bradbury, Blackley, and Bertram, were working on the premises from 5 a.m. till 8 p.m., while the acting secretary, Mr. Thompson, installed a bed in his office in order to be there day and night. The much needed services of an assistant butcher were obtained during the third week, but even then the strain on the butchers was tremendous. Considerable relief was given to the overworked staff by the re-opening of the markets a fortnight ago. However, even now with fewer customers and more coolie labour, it is still impossible to supply cooked stuff, while sausages, corned beef and dripping can only be prepared at spasmodic intervals.

Our reporter was greatly surprised at the amount of work performed there behind the scenes from 6 a.m. till 5 p.m. shipping orders, hotel orders, club and hospital orders, Shameen and Cheung Chau orders, splitting up frozen carcasses with mighty cleavers, branch orders, etc., etc. As he said: "What would we have done without the Dairy Farm?"

Should your piece of beef or mutton not be the cut you specially like or what you have been in the habit of getting from the Dairy Farm Company, remember it is strike time, consider the long hours these butchers are working, and in your hearts render thanks to the overworked men of Pokfulam, Wyndham Street, and East Point Ice Depot.

headline: REPRESENTATIONS TO BE MADE.
text:
The tightness of the money market formed the chief subject of discussion at a meeting of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce yesterday afternoon.

The Chairman, Mr. Li You-chuen, said his attention had been drawn to the fact that owing to the property slump, many banks had suspended connection with their clients. His personal opinion was that considered generally the tightness of the money market could hardly be avoided but things might, however, be improved if proper arrangements were made with the compradores of the Banks. It had been suggested that one of the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council might be requested to approach the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce, the managers of the Banks and others in order that satisfactory arrangements might be made.

The meeting eventually agreed to appoint members in connection with such negotiations; Mr. J. M. Wong to represent the Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Mr. Mok Ching-pong to represent the banking circle (Mr. Ho Sai-wing, the compradore of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, having previously declined to serve).

In the course of further discussion it was stated that a contributory factor in the bringing about of a tightness of the money market was the prohibition on free movement of goods and it was agreed that the Government should be requested to consider permitting the export of goods which represented the lifeblood of the Colony.

A unanimous decision was also passed emphasising that the strike was caused by intimidation carried out by a small section of the labouring community and did not represent the wishes of the merchants.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—Some people do not care one way or the other whether the remaining river boats continue operations or not. Others do care. There are yet others who, by virtue of long contact with the crews, are able to throw light on one aspect of the trouble as the men concerned themselves are far too much scared to do anything.

Strike Executive are calling on the No. 1's of the crews. On introduction they take considerable pains to explain that they are volunteers, duly empowered by the Executive, the members of the latter having had to make themselves scarce. I have recognised one or two of these "volunteers" as former No. 1's on river and coastal shipping. As they are out of work themselves they are anxious to see all colleagues idle. After a brief hurangue on national honour, they emphasise the claim that if all shipping was to cease the trouble would soon be over. As is characteristic of the Chinese worker, the men approached put off the agitators by promising that if vital lines shut down, they will also stop themselves. In this manner, one has been waiting for the other and the service has continued till now. If a visit were paid to the ships an hour or two after arrival at the wharves here some of these "volunteer" delegates could be seen actually making their daily rounds. To those who have been ap

To those who have been approached I would say that it is difficult to see how the situation up North can be affected by making the shipping stoppage an entire one.

Thanking you for inserting this letter.

Yours, etc.,

(To the Editor of The China Mail)

Sir,—Perhaps the thought may have struck others or the suggestion I am about to make has already been put into actual practice. With regard to the letter published in your issue of yesterday, from “An Americann Friend,” I beg to propose, with all deference, that the Government have the letter translated and re-published (1) in the vernicular papers which are still being issued and (2) as circulars as was the case with a speech of Mr. D. Lloyd George at a critical period of the last War. Such publication may do a great deal to commenter pernicious propaganda from sources beyond the control of the Colony.

About the question of reward for arrests and/or convictions of agitators. There are some of us who may think twice about performing a public duty because a wrong impression may be gained, viz. that of going after the monetary reward. Such people would consider a medal or other tangible remembrance a much more suitable reward.

Yours, etc.

headline: HELD UP:
text:
INCIDENTS AT SHANGHAI

Shanghai: July 7.

The shipping situation remains the same and the concentrated intimidation of the last few days resulted in a number of tramwaymen failing to turn up this morning, but the Tramway Company is determined to carry on. Specials guarded the trams to-day. There was no incident. Otherwise, however, the situation is quiet, though forty thousand are out of work due to the cutting off of the bulk of the power supply of electricity. In many cases resumption is believed to be taking place owing to the inadequate dole which is being given out.

The bulk of the power supply of electricity has been discontinued. A number of mills are installing their own motors.

Agitators are taking advantage of the discontinuance of the electricity supply and are furthering unrest, but no serious trouble has occurred.

The intimidation of tramwaymen is being carried on without abatement. Last evening, a crowd of a hundred, including a number of former tramwaymen, held up a car conveying thirty tramway fitters from the repair shops. They forced the fitters to accompany them to Chinese territory.

About half the telephone operators have resumed work.

The body of an American member of the crew of the s.s. President Pierce has been found in a creek, whilst a British blue-jacket has been missing for sixty hours and has not yet been found.

At the inquest on the man who was shot by the American seaman Dizik, it was stated that the deceased was shot by the sailor when the latter was protecting a Municipal officer. Two men who were arrested were charged at the Mixed Court, one for inciting to riot and the other for firing crackers. The first was remandied on bail, and the other nominally fined.

The Japanese community is raising subscriptions for the purpose of making a presentation to the Volunteers and naval landing parties in recognition of their services. So far, nearly ten thousand dollars have been subscribed.

headline: Chungking Unrest.
text:
A wireless message from Chungking, dated July 6, says the Japanese concession was surrounded by a crowd all day long. The Japanese Consul considers that a collision is likely. The authorities have not taken effective action.

Reports from Hoihow and Pakhoi'say Chinese gunboats are expected to arrive shortly.

Ningpo is reported quiet. The local authorities are prepared to provide protection.

headline: Dosser Trial.
text:
Shanghai; July 7..

The Mixed Court dismissed three of the four charges against Dosser who was allowed bail on Tls. 20,000 security (which the Soviet Trade Mission is alleged to be furnishing).

Dosser, was remanded for a week. All charges against his wife were dismissed. The remaining charge against Dosser is that he made preparations to openly incite disorder.

The Court dismissed the charge that accused was making preparations to commit a hostile-act against certain foreign states, because the text of an article in the Chinese Criminal Code, whereon the charge was based, meant "declare war" and not "hostile act." Two other charges were dismissed as they rested upon the above mentioned charge.

headline: THE PARADE.
text:
The naval, military, and Volunteer units made a brave show as they paraded the streets yesterday afternoon.

The regular naval and military units marched through the West Point district and the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps through the Wanchai and Causeway Bay district.

headline: GANDE, PRICE & CO., LTD. WINN MINEOIANTS
CANTON POSITION. / PROSPECTS OF WARFARE.
text:
General Li Fook-lam, the "governor" of Honum which is on the opposite side of the River to Canton, has, it is stated, forbidden strikers to land in his territory for fear that they may be agents of the Reds, or the so-called Leftists of the Kuomintang party.

Martial law has been declared and is strictly enforced, says the "China Mail" Canton correspondent. To the eye it does not appear as if the Leftists will take up arms against the anti-nationalisation of property clique of whom General Li is said to be a leader with General Hsu Shung-chi, commander-in-chief.

No matter what way the trend of politics may be following, General Li has tried to keep the strikers from Hongkong and Shameen at arm's length.

Hongkong verinacular papers report that General Cheung Kai-sleak, now one of the most powerful of the Leftists and the commander of the "Whampoa Cadets" is organising his forces so as to make a clean sweep for Communism. An offensive from Whampoa to Honam is stated to have been planned.

Taking the various reports con- junctively it seems that although the politicians have patched matters up, the militarists are not content to leave important questions in suspense.

Some of the local vernacular papers have also published reports of the alleged taking over of the Kung Yee (Hospital) in Canton by the administration. The Kung Yee is reported to have large sources of revenue and the stated reason for Government control is that the Kwangtung University is to be run in conjunction with the hospital. In one source it is mentioned that the hospital properties are worth about a million dollars. Added significance is given by the return to Hongkong of Dr. S. F. Lee, former superintendent of the hospital.

headline: IN EARNEST. / WHAT STRIKERS ARE LEARNING.
text:
NAVAL YARD EXAMPLE

That employers were in earnest when they warned employees of the dire results to themselves which would follow absorption from work is proved by the fact that they have adhered steadily to that policy and that strikers who have returned or attempted to return have been informed that they must commence again as beginners in their particular class of work.

That many of them were unacquainted with British methods, and imagined that the warning was just bluff, is also proved by the astonishment with which they have received the news of the employers' adherence to their previously announced policy. This has been so in the case of the Hotels Company and the Naval Yard, and doubtless it will be the case when Harbour office employees, coxswains, etc., present themselves for re-employment and this in spite of the clearness with which the Harbour Master made the position clear to them. The Star Ferry workers will also have to start on the lowest scale of wages, and doubtless the same astonishment will be manifested by them.

Of the 200 workers who have returned to the Naval Yard all but a dozen or so have reconciled themselves to the inevitable and have remained in the knowledge that half a loaf is better than no bread. Not all of them, however, will be able to find reemployment just yet even at the lowest scale. In normal times about 2,000 are employed, but the largest number, which can be usefully employed at the moment is 500. Those returning at the Yard appear to be coming in batches of grades, the first being the engine fitters and the next the carpenters, this pointing to some arrangement by which a consensus of opinion of these different branches is taken.

Peking, July 16.—The vernacular papers report that the Waichiaopu has protested to the Diplomatic body recently regarding the Shanghai Council cutting off electric light. Sig. Cerruti is reported to have replied but the nature of the reply is not announced.—Reuter.

headline: GETTING OUT.
text:
STRIKERS EVADE CANTON TICKETS.

ROUNDABOUT ROUTES.

In spite of the activity of pickots in Canton, individual workmen are escaping from the fold and even getting down to Hongkong by circuitous routes, writes the "China Mail" correspondent.

Practically everybody with the appearance of a striker who passes along the Canton Bund is closely examined by pickets in uniform and the first question is "Are you trying to get to Hongkong? If so the person, man or woman, is taken to Strike Headquarters on the second band for "trial."

Although river steamer traffic between Hongkong and Canton has raised up with the exception of the Hong Kong there are still means of travelling. It is reported that pickets are also on duty at Taishatan, the terminal of the Canton-Kowloon Railway, to prevent the rank and file deserting by that route. To circumvent the agitators, smokers have first left Canton by tow-boats which ply to all points in the delta. After reaching an intermediary point "defaults" go on by another towboat to Macao where steamers convey them to Hongkong. The s.s. Anjo and No Chow have been running between Hongkong and Macao this week. It is the same with the railway. Strikers leave by tow-boat for a point near the Boea Tigris Forts, tranship inland and board a train in Chinese territory for Samchun. There is undoubtedly evidence, adds the correspondent, that unrest is spreading, particularly with the cargo coolies who have complained of bad guild management on their own pipt and preferential treatment to flavoured guilds by the

It appears that when the coolies struck sympathetically with the scamer in the last exodus from Hongkong, the same thing happened. At that time seamen were enjoying themselves in flower-boats and having picnies on the river while the coolies had to live in temporary shacks by the side of the Bund. This time, the seamen are alleged to be receiving both meals and "tea-money" while the outsiders' grumble at inferior quarters and irregular food.

headline: STRIKE NEWS. / CHINESE ASPECT IMPROVES.
text:
During the last two days, the number of tea-houses, restaurants and eating houses which have resumed business, has been constantly increasing. Some of the establishments have only a very limited menu, "devoid of variety owing to the absence of cooks who are away, and who find difficulty in getting back.

The majority of native barber hops have also re-opened their oors.

Every day the vernacular press announces new bodies of special guards organised by Chinese communities to assist in preserving the peace. A suggestion has now been made that the district special guards also supervise that part of sanitation relating to the disposal of nightsoil as the poorer classes are not aware of the arrangements made.

Nightsoil coolies are also returning to their jobs especially in the central district and in Yaumati.

Yesterday the Chinese Trade Maintenance Association elected Mr. Ho Kwong as chairman, with headquarters on the first floor of the City Hall. Chinese merchants who experience difficulty in connection with merchandise, transport, etc. are asked to report to the Association, at City Hall, at 11 a.m. each day, and they will be assisted as far as possible.

Brokenhill, N. Rhodesia, July 16.—The Prince of Wales who leaves Capetown on July 29 for South America has completed his programme in North Rhodesia, the main feature of which was the meeting of the native chiefs in all parts of the territory whom the Prince lengthily and impressively addressed. Thereafter the Prince opened the hydro-electric scheme at Mulungushi whereby a narrow river in the heart of Central Africa will be converted into a mighty lake, usable for generating power. The Prince congratulated all concerned in the affair and also acknowledged the courtesy of the Belgian Government in sending the Governor of Katanga to greet him.—Reuter.

headline: CHINESE AFFAIRS.
text:
CONSULAR AND NAVAL PROTECTION.

In the House of Commons, the Rt. Hon. Ronald McNeill, replying to an enquiry regarding the recent Shanghai disturbances, said Mr. Austen Chamberlain hoped the House would permit him to defer further statements on Chinese affairs until communications between the interested Powers had reached a point when a full statement can be made with due regard to public interest and international comity.

Replying to Colonel Grant Morden (Con.) with regard to the protection of British missionaries in China, Mr. McNeill stated the Chinese authorities had been reminded of their responsibilities as regards the safety of Britishers in China, and Consular Officers and Naval forces in China will afford British subjects all possible protection. Presumably in connection with the discussion of the Chinese situation, the American, French and Japanese Ambassadors jointly conferred with Mr. Chamberlin at the Foreign Office today.

headline: U.S.A. IN ACCORD
text:
Reuter learns that the latest indications from America show the United States is entirely in accord with Britain in regard to China. The general line of policy of both is to push on as rapidly as possible the Washington Conference programme when conditions in China are favourable for such a step.

It seems obvious the tariffs Conference will necessarily precede any conference on extra-territoriality and it seems likely that the body which will ultimately deal with the latter will be a committee of preliminary investigation into the circus riots.

headline: RIFF WAR.
text:
MARSHAL PETAIN FOR MOROCCO.

Marshal Petain has departed for Morocco to confer with Marshall Lyautey regarding the measures to be taken against the Riffs.

.Reinforcements continue to be sent to Morocco.

[Marshal Petain won fame in the Great War as one of the most brilliant of French generals.]

Earlier messages stated:— Paris, July 16. — Newspapers announce that a party of American airmen (twelve, according to the Hayas Agency) have offered their services to France against the Riffs. M. Painleve accepted a squadron which proceeds to Fez within a fortnight. According to messages from Fez the reinforcements expected in Morocco amount to an army corps. Abdel Krim has refused to accept the armistice communiqué and says that pressure continues in the centre where the French detachments are unceasingly under fire. Enemy infiltrations continue preparatory to an expected offensive.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir, it seems quite certain that it will be impossible to carry through this settlement on July 21 as now proposed by the Government as no money is available for that purpose and the banks are not giving any financial facilities, and a great many Chinese clients are away, or cannot be found at present. The Government, as already pointed out in your columns, would seem to be acting only in the interests of a small minority (10 per cent) who have made money by selling forward, and quite ignore the interests of the remaining 90 per cent., who (both brokers and clients) would be saddled with enormous liabilities, which they will never be able to pay.

The more one considers the question the plainer it seems that the only proper solution is to cancel all contracts for July/September, as by doing so no one would really be money out of pocket.

headline: UNANIMOUS DECISIONS. / YESTERDAY'S STRIKE MEETING PACKED
text:
The City Hall was filled to over- flowing yesterday before the hour at which the Community Meeting was due to com- mence and a move was therefore made to the Theatre Royal where here, again, the capacity was taxed to its utmost. The meeting was characterised by absolute unanimity. Governor

The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Chairman, was greeted with loud cheers on rising to address the meeting.

He referred to the fact that this was the second time in less than three years that the (Colony had been called upon to face a strike which was bound to have disastrous economic effects on the Chinese and on ourselves. The workers did not want to strike. The memories and discomforts of the last strike and the non-fulfilment of false promises by the labour unions were too fresh in the memories of most of them to do so. Yet, at the bidding of alien agitatoffs from Cantori and as the result of intimidation they fled in terror and for five weeks we have been dealing with the consequences. The resolutions were proposed not in any spirit of antagonism to our ancient Chinese friends, but with the sincere belief that by the eradication of the Bolsheviks from their midst lies not only the hope of international salvation in all dealings with China but the preservation of her own rights and country from utter destruction. (Applause).

"1. It is recommended that no wages be paid for June to returning strikers and that careful revision of terms and conditions be made upon their re-employment."

No Weakness. In support of this resolution I may state that in the first place the law says it is unnecessary to pay any wages for June, and that you can even recover damages from the servant who has left without warning. In the second place I know—and I think I may fairly say that I am authorised to state—that the principle of the Government institutions throughout the Colony, be it the Civil Government, the Army or Navy, is that no returning striker will be employed unless he is absolutely essential, and that in that case he will only be employed on a lower grade than that at which he left. (Applause.) Far be it from me to advocate a policy of retaliation, but as I have said before, this is the second strike within three years. The settlement of the last strike was responsible for very many servants and employees going out. In the usual British way we were a little soft and a little over-just and generous in the settlement which was made on that occasion, and we hoped it might never occur again. It has occurred again, and without any desire to be vindictive, I think that the Colony ought to see that these strikes cannot recur without the consequences being placed upon those who provoke them. (Applause). I have already stated, and I believe to be a fact, that those who left our employment, were the dupes of a spirit of intrigue which brought them out, and might possibly have brought them out in spite of anything and everything we could have done in this Colony to prevent it. Nevertheless, ladies and gentlemen, I think it is desirable that we should register our feeling upon that point with the spirit certainly of justice and possibly of mercy, but with a little less mercy than we registered last time, because it was abused (Applause).

Mr. W. S. Bailey said: Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen, I have much pleasure in seconding this resolution. These strikers have done their utmost to paralyze our trade. No business or Colony can exist indefinitely without adequate income. The economic losses of both European and Chinese businesses are alike very heavy and must seriously react on staffs employed and on wages paid for some time to come.

There appears no just cause for this strike, the employees having absolutely nothing of which to complain. British firms, especially British shipping firms, the most liberal and generous of employers, distributing yearly thousands of dollars gratuity to employees, together with other benefits—these firms have been discriminated against and all their vessels abandoned while rival vessels under the Chinese flag and paying lower wages have been allowed to run.

Businesses in the Colony, both Chinese and European, have lost money right through this stricken land. and have paid salaries and wages not from profit but from capital, thereby reducing the earnings of these businesses and preventing them, however-willing-they-maybe, from giving employees in future the same liberal terms and gratuities as formerly.
Endorsed.

An attempt has been made to starve us out financially by cutting off our sources of income. That attempt has only failed of complete success by the splendid unselfish work of our own people, our own residents of all races, and by the loyal service of the many Chinese workers who have stood so faithfully by us. With such complete unity and cheerful determination as has been shown we could never be beaten, but surely our first duty is to reward those who have so worked for us and not the strikers whose action has so deeply injured both us and them. (Applause).

There may be some who would formerly have dealt even more lawlessly with strikers, but later developments have certainly warranted their adoption of a stronger attitude in this respect. By leaving without notice strikers have dismissed themselves and are liable to forfeiture of a month's pay in lieu of notice and to prosecution, and it would be due to us and due to our loyal employees that returning strikers be dealt with thus strictly according to British law, otherwise there could be no security for future traders or workers of any nationality in the Colony. But justice should be tempered with mercy and we ask only the cancellation of the striker's wages for June, although we cannot forget that the mercy shown by us after the strike of 1922 was apparently mistaken for weakness on our part.

Let us be merciful as expressed by the resolution, but strong and ust. just to ourselves, to our lives and families and to our loyal workers who have so suffered and ill suffer by this strike.

I know ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to support our laws and Government and support the interest of our own people and our loyal helpers by voting unanimously for the resolution. (Applause).

The resolution was carried with enthusiastic unanimity.

headline: Registration.
text:
The following resolution was then before the meeting for consideration:—

"2. This meeting requests the Hongkong Government to cooperate in the establishment of a voluntary system of registration of office employees and domestic servants."

The Chairman briefly stated that he believed in a voluntary system of registration, not a compulsory one which would involve penalties on both sides in certain eventualities.

The Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird said: Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen, in rising to second the resolution now before the meeting, I do not for one moment suggest that if the registration of domestic servants becomes an accomplished fact, it will prove to be a panacea for all our troubles, but it is my honest belief that it would be to the general benefit of the community if registration were undertaken on the right lines. We should think of those who are coming after us and endeavour to make this type of so-called strike, where the actual strikers had no grievance, more difficult. Although I do not suggest that such registration would stop strikes, it is my opinion that it would be a partial safeguard. It would be a form of combination on the part of employers to counter the combination of employees, and that is recognized all the world over as equitable. (Applause).

The objections to registration which I have heard expressed, and read of in the papers, do not strike me as very serious. I cannot see why it should cause discontent. All of us have been accustomed ever since the war began, to obtain passports with our photographs in duplicate. We submit without a murmur to the indignity of stating our ages, our physical disabilities, our distinguishing marks (Laughter)—why should Chinese domestics take these matters more to heart than we do? (Applause).

There is in force at the moment compulsory registration for Europeans, by the police authorities, in connection with essential services. All-domestics—at—home have a form of registration under the National Insurance Act. Moreover it is the custom here with a number of the large business concerns to register all their Chinese staff who are in permanent employ. Furthermore, all indentured labour is registered through the S.C.A., and I am told there is never a murmur against it.

As regards finger prints I do not consider that is absolutely necessary. The photograph in duplicate, one on the card to be filed at the Bureau, and the other on the card held by the domestic, is all that would be necessary, and it could be made an offence punishable by a fine for any one to tamper with a registration card.

Because the law has been in- operativa in Ceylon, as we are told, only seems to me to show that it is no longer necessary there, and should such registration become law in this Colony it will probably die a natural death if it is found there is no longer any call for it.

To my mind it is necessary that this registration if carried out should be done by the Government. There is no reason for it to be a financial drag on the Colony, for the fees for registration should far more than pay for the personnel of the office. A registry office run as a private concern does not appeal to me. I have had some experience of such offices, and from the attitude of some of them it would seem that it is to their interest for one to change one's servants as often as possible. (Laughter.)

As regards an employer giving a servant a bad character without due cause, I think it will be found that people are too afraid of the law of libel to make that objection a serious one.

As regards written characters these are useless unless accompanied by a photograph, as one never knows whether the character produced was ever written for the individual who presents it. The ones use dare generally written by a resident who has long since left the Colony, so that there is no means of verifying same.

Ladies and Gentlemen, I am still to be convinced that there is any valid objection to the official registration of servants save the trouble entailed and if it is to the interest of the community that it should be undertaken, then that objection should be over-ruled. With these remarks, Sir, I have much pleasure in seconding the resolution now before the meeting. (Applause).

Mr. J. Russell (Taikoo) and Mr. L. M. Whyte contributed to the discussion, the former suggesting that registration should be arranged by the Residents' Associations. The Chairman said that he did not think there was the slightest hope of legislation being introduced at the present time but if it was proved that there was sufficient interest in voluntary registration the Government might be encouraged to go further with it.

The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously:

headline: China Business.
text:
Following was the next resolution to be considered:—

That in view of the extremely heavy losses being suffered by all British traders here and in China, present negotiations should be accelerated as much as possible, consistently with retaining all treaty rights, but it is the unanimous opinion of this meeting that no discussion concerning revised customs tariff or extraterritoriality should be begun whilst anti-foreign disturbances or boycotts continue in any part of China or Hongkong.

The Chairman briefly referred to the seriousness of the situation for merchants throughout China, and Mr. J. Owen Hughes, in seconding, attributed the present trouble to forces outside the Colony. Residents of long standing knew full well the worth of the Chinese merchants, and in this trouble it could not be made too clear that we had no quarrel whatsoever with the Chinese. The resolution was carried unanimously.

The fourth resolution read as follows:—

4. That having regard to the recent criticisms in the House of Commons concerning emergency regulations enacted by the Governor in Council to deal with abnormal and threatening conditions, this meeting desires to express the approval of the entire foreign community and all right thinking Chinese, of such regulations as being absolutely necessary under the circumstances, and the entire confidence of the community in the actions of the Governor throughout this crisis, and is of opinion that his firm attitude and strong measures have thus far prevented a serious outbreak of violence.

The Chairman referred to the attacks made by the Labour party at Home on the Emergency Regulations passed by the Hongkong Government, the sacrificing of his home leave by His Excellency the Governor and the measures taken by the Governor-in-Council to deal with the situation. Bolsheviks Elements. The Hon Mr C G Alabaster, in seconding the resolution said that it was only right that because His Excellency at the beginning of the strike informed the community of Hongkong that he and his Government were ready to stand shoulder to shoulder with the law-abiding elements in this Colony, that the law-abiding elements in this Colony should now tell the House of Commons that we stand shoulder to shoulder with him and his Government. (Applause):

Mr. Alabaster referred to the attempts that had been made by an external Government for the utilisation of every anti-foreign element and every Bolshevistic element that could be laid hands on to destroy the very foundations of life and business in the Colony. It was necessary for the Government to counter these measures and the distribution to loyal employees of threatening leaflets, and it was hardly to be wondered at that paid intimidators who had been foiled by the mere introduction of the emergency regulation relating to the imposition of the cat, should telegraph to the Labour Party in London to protest against the cruelty of the Hongkong Government.

Mr. W. H. Bell supported the resolution and it also was carried unanimously.

Following is the fifth resolution then before the Council:—

5. That this meeting desires to point out to the Home Government that the Shameen-Canton question will probably require to be dealt with, separately and in consultation with the Hongkong Government, whose interests are equally vital with those of the Foreign Office in all South China questions, especially as the present Canton Government will probably refuse to recognise any agreement reached with the Central Government in Peking. The situation in Hongkong and South China has been entirely provoked by Bolshevik influence and intrigue and is aggressively Communistic and violently anti-British. This meeting therefore urges His Majesty's Government to take strong and immediate action to protect British lives, property and trade in Hongkong and China by at once increasing the strength of the China Squadron in river gunboats and aircraft-carriers, and that, additionally, a battalion of British troops, should be transferred to Hongkong at the earliest possible moment for use here or in any part of China as emergency requires. Finally, it respectfully urges that His Majesty's Government should immediately inform the de facto Government in Canton that unless it withdraws its support, of the attack upon British interests, that they will be regarded as having entered into a state of hostility with the British Government.

In bringing this resolution forward the Chairman said that the Home Government must recognise that the problems of Canton and Hongkong could not be divorced, and if the Canton problem was referred to Peking without consulting Hongkong, it would be ludicrous. and farcical. (Applause.) The people at Home must realise that though the Shanghai dispute might be settled, the Bolshevik Government of Canton would probable refuse to recognise anything done in Peking. In the settlement Hongkong could not be left out. (Cheers.)

headline: Sir H. Pollock's Views.
text:
Sir Henry Pollock, in second, spoke of the operation in the Colony and in China of the hidden hand of Bolshevism and asked if we were going to allow the interests which had been built up here to be destroyed at the bidding of the Bolshevists. Giving reasons why the Chinese community had confidence in the fairness and protection of the Hongkong Government, the speaker said that the Chinese, from the highest to the lowest, from the richest merchant to the humblest coolie, have a special office, the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs, to which they can send in requests for the removal of any supposed grievances or injustice. Those requests, if in the Chinese language, are translated into English, and in many cases finally reach the Governor in Council; and I can testify personally, as a Member of that Council, of many years standing that the most careful and impartial attention is paid to the representations of all Chinese, however humble their station. Furthermore the Hongkong Government is in constant consultation with the Chinese members of the Legislative Council, who take great pains to ascertain the general feeling of the Chinese Community in this Colony. The periodical large influxes of Chinese with their families into Hongkong in times of disturbance in the neighbouring Republic of China afford yet further proof, if any such be required, of the confidence of the Chinese people in the fairness of protection of our Government. In short, Hongkong is a splendid and wonderful example of the

operation, and of the harmonious working together of the British and Chinese residents under the reign of law and order, which has been maintained here during the past 85 years by civil Servants of the highest integrity and impartiality. Are we going to allow this splendid British Colony which has been built up with such patience and labour and our commerce and credit not only here but all over China to be destroyed at the bidding of Bolsheviks? Are we going, at Bolshevik dictation, to give up the results of the strenuous labour of three generations of our countrymen in this Colony and in Shanghai and other parts of China, the labourers of our Civil Servants, Municipal Councillors, Ministers, Consuls, Commissioners of Customs, merchants and others?

In conclusion, Sir Henry said that it seemed clear that, in default of joint action by the other Powers concerned, the duty rests upon Great Britain, in the interests of civilization and of the national reconstruction of China upon correct lines to take action by herself, if necessity arises.

headline: GOOD FEELING.
text:
MERCHANTS' WITH, BRITAIN

CHINESE RELATIONS

STRIKE NOT WANTED.

At an extraordinary meeting of the Trade Maintenance Bureau presided over by Mr. Ho Kwong on Saturday, Mr. Ho Iu said that ever since the establishment of the Trade Maintenance Bureau, all merchants alike were deeply appreciative of the services rendered by this organization to relieve the situation, brought about by the strikes in Hongkong. The Bureau had succeeded in getting the Nam Pak Hong tallymen and the cargo coolies ashore and afloat to resume work, namely, to discharge and loaded cargo, etc.

As the foreign firms in the Colony are the principal ship owners, and there is no denying the fact that the shipping of the Port is entirely in their hands, representation, he thought should be made by this Bureau to the British Chamber of Commerce regarding taking on new crews for steamers lying idle in the Harbour so as to facilitate the speedier sailing of steamers. This being done, the shipping of the Port would be brought back to its normal conditions, so that a free movement of merchandise would ensue.

Dwelling further, upon the strike, Mr. Ho Iu said that ever since the similar trouble broke out in the Northern Settlement, the feeling of foreigners towards the Chinese was none too friendly. Hongkong being a British Colony with a cosmopolitan population, wherein foreigners and Chinese have much to do with each other in their trade intercourse, Mr. Ho Iu was anxious that no misunderstanding should arise between them. As the meeting of this Bureau was largely represented by the commercial community, he would suggest that a general meeting of the Twenty-Four Trade Merchants Guilds, as well as a meeting of the General Chinese Chamber of Commerce, should be convened to enable the Chinese in this Colony to give expression to their opinions regarding the strike. Mention should be made that the strike was initiated entirely at the instigation of the communistic intimidators outside, quite beyond the control and jurisdiction of the Hongkong Government. Their sole object was to deal a deadly blow to the finance and commerce of the Colony. The merchants were heart and soul against it and he, the speaker, considered that the Hongkong Government should be approached with a view to requesting it to convey by telegram to the Home Government the cordial feeling of the Chinese merchants towards the British Government and people in general. Mr. Ho Kwong thought that this was an excellent idea and said he would lose no time in conferring with Mr. Li Yau-chuen, chairman of the General Chinese Chamber of Commerce, so that a meeting might be called at once.

headline: HARBOUR CHASE.
text:
CHARGE AGAINST A BOATMAN.

EUROPEAN'S COMPLAINT.

A Chinese boatman was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning with using obscene language.

The complainant, Mr. E. L. Stainfield, stated in evidence that he was travelling by the "Star" ferry from Kowloon to Hongkong on Saturday afternoon and in the middle of the harbour the accused used an indecent expression after posting himself at the rear of a passing junk. Witness later engaged a motor bout and in company with his wife and Mr. W. Anderson of the Naval Hospital overhauled the junk near Arsenal Street. Witness stated that the accused jumped into the harbour as soon as he boarded the junk and repeated the expression used.

Accused denied that he used the alleged expression, and explained his fall into the sea by stating that he was assaulted by the complainant and pushed overboard.

The case was adjourned until to-morrow for the examination of other witnesses.

headline: TO-DAY'S WEDDING. / BURLING—HILL.
text:
St. John's Cathedral was the scene of a pretty wedding this afternoon, the parties being Miss Gwendoline Hill, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. G. S. Hill, and Mr. W. J. Burling, son of the late Mr. and Mrs. Burling.

The Rev. G. T. Waldegrave officiated.

The bride was given away by her father and looked charming in a dress of white satin and ivory silk lace, tulle veil and "orange blossoms. She carried a bouquet of roses.

Her attendants were Miss Gladys Brock and Miss Doreen Spanton, bridesmaids, who were attired in mauve morocain dresses with hats to match and whose bouquets were also of roses.

The bride's mother wore a dress of nigger brown Paris crepe with silk lace to match and brown hat.

The best man was Mr. A. Mandell.

After a reception at the Hong- kong Hotel the happy couple are to leave for Repulse Bay where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress is of saxe blue Paris crepe with hat to match.

The presents received were numerous and valuable.

headline: LOCAL WEDDING / DYER—BOTT.
text:
A pretty wedding took place at Union Church, Kennedy Road, on Saturday afternoon, the bride and bridegroom being Miss Grace Bott, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. W. Bott, Guildborough, Northampton, and Sergt. W. A. Dyer of the Central Police Headquarters, son of Mr. and Mrs. William White Dyer, Northwood, England.

The bride arrived in Hongkong on Thursday by the s.s. Macedonia.

The officiating clergyman was the Rev. J. H. Johnstone.

The bride was given away by Principal Warder W. Y. Robertson, and was, charmingly attired in a primrose and heliotrope georgette dress with hat to match. The pearl necklace she wore was the gift of the bridegroom. The attendant of the bride was Mrs. W. Robertson, who was dressed in manure cigarette.

Sergt. C. J. Kingdon, of the Hongkong Police Force was best man.

The wedding ceremony was followed by a reception held at the home of Mrs. W. Y. Robertson after which the bride and bridegroom left for Repulse Bay where the honeymoon is being spent. The brides going away dress was of blue Shantung and crepe de chine.

Many presents were received.

text:

headline: “HELL'S KITCHEN.”
text:
BATTLING SIKI STABBED IN NEW YORK.

CONDITION SERIOUS.

The Senegalese pugilist Batling Siki has been found unconscious.

He was stabbed in the neck in a street in the "Hell's Kitchen" quarter. He is in hospital in a serious condition.

[Siki leapt into fame by a dramatic, though questioned, defeat of Georges Carpentier, one time idol of France.]

Punch Ball

Golf

The scores in each instance, it will be admitted, speak for themselves, and it would be superfluous to describe either match in detail.

The baseballers, however, are to be complimented on setting the lead in the matter of resumption of Saturday afternoon sport in spite of the strike, and now that they have shown the way there is no doubt that other forms of sport will be revived. After holding a number of important traffic positions on the Rad Lines, he was, in 1901, appointed Fourth Vice-President, the Charge of Rad Traffic; in 1910, he was appointed Vice-President. headline: NO NEW PEERS.
text:
An unusually long Birthday Honours List does not contain any new peers though it promotes Baron Beursted to a Viscount Sir William Tyrrell steps up to the Grand Cross of the Most Distinguished Order of St. Michael and St. George. Sir William Pakenham gets a Grand Cross of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath (G.C.B.)

Eight baronetcies include Sir John Bland Sutton.

The long list of knighthoods for varied public services include the artist Bernard Partridge and Mr. Philip Smith, Grand Secretary of the United Grand Lodge of Freemasons.

A notable feature is several pages of Orders of the British Empire (G.B.E., K.B.E., D.B.E., C.B.E., O.B.E., and M.B.E.) including six dames.

headline: Baron Beurstec
text: Baron Bearsted, who has been made a viscount, is well-known in the metropolis, having held the post of Lord Mayor, Alderman and Sheriff. He has travelled extensively in Japan and the Far East and was the first to introduce the transport of petrol in bulk through the Suez Canal. He has developed large oil fields in the Far East and received an official vote of thanks from the Lord. Commissioner of the Admiralty during the war for "services of the utmost importance to the fighting forces.

headline: Sir William Tyrrell
text: Sir William Tyrell's connection with the Foreign Office dates back nearly forty years. He is the son of the late Judge of the High Court of Judicature, N.W. Provinces of India. Since 1919 he has carried out the duties of Assistant Under-Secretary of State at the Foreign Office. He has also acted as Private Secretary to Lord Saunderson and the Right Hon Sir Edward Grey and 2nd Secretary at the Embassy at Rome. Sir William has received a G.C.M.G.

headline: Sir William Pakenham
text: Admiral Sir William Pakenham, given the Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath, comes of an old family with seafaring traditions. His father was Rear-Admiral the Hon. Thomas Pakenham and at an early age the son saw service in Japan and China as a naval attache. During the war he rose from Captain to Vice-Admiral and Lord Commissioner of the Admiralty. As a Rear-Admiral he commanded the Battle Cruiser Fleet.

headline: Sir John Bland Sutton.
text: Sir John Bland Sutton is one of the leading surgeons of the day and in connection with the R.A.M.C. in the War rendered services of great national importance. He has since been elected to the "Presidency of the Royal College of Surgeons. He is said to have made large gifts to needy hospitals. Sir John Sutton was trained at Middlesex Hospital at which he was afterwards surgeon.

Sir John Baird receives the Grand Cross of St. Michael and St. George (G.C.M.G.)

The Earl of Lonsdale.

The Earl of Lonsdale is Lord Lieut. of Cumberland and his magnificent country seat at Lowther Castle is a very popular summer resort for Royalty. Lord Lonsdale has been an ardent sportsman all his life, taking a particular interest in the turf, hunting and boxing. His name is most prominently connected in public memory with the Lonsdale belt he founded. He served in the Imperial Yeomanry during the Boer War. For two years he was Mayor of Whitehaven.

headline: Lớnd Desborough.
text: As Chairman of the Primrose League, and Thames Conservancy Board, also as a member of the Tariff Commission and Royal Exhibitions Commission, Lord Desborough has done work of great national importance but his name is more popularly connected with the British Olympic Association in which he has been a presiding genius. As Mr. W. H. Grenfell he had once a wonderful athletic record at cricket, rowing, running, climbing, swimming and horsemanship.

headline: Sir John L. Baird.
text: Born in 1874. He was a secretary in the Diplomatic Service in Cairo, Paris, and Buenos Aires from 1898 to 1908; Attached at Vienna in 1896; Acting Agent and Consul-General in Abyssinia; and Political Officer attached to the Abyssinian Field Forces in 1903. From 1911 until 1916 he was Parliamentary private secretary to Mr. Bonar Law; from December, 1916, until January, 1919, was Under-Secretary of State for the Air Ministry, and from July, 1919, Under-Secretary for the Home Office. He has represented the Rugby Division since 1910.

headline: DASH TO THE POLE. / PLANES TO TAKE PART
text:
AMUNDSEN RETURNING AFOOT?

The Government has decided to send two naval aeroplanes by steamer to Spitzbergen to assist in the search for Amundsen.

The aeroplanes will reach Spitzbergen at the end of next week.

The opinion is generally expressed that Amundsen has been unable to return by air and is making for Cape Columbia or Spitzbergen on foot.

headline: LATEST NOTE. / EFFORT TO CONCILIATE GERMANY.
text:
DISARMAMENT QUESTION.

The Allied Note to Germany with regard to dis-armament, which will be presented to Berlin on June 4, consists of five pages and two annexes.

The first sets out what has been done and what has not been done in the execution of the Versailles Treaty and lays down a list of what remains to be carried out.

The second gives the text of the Reparations' Commissions note to the Conference of Ambassadors, declaring that Germany is in order as regards the execution of the Dawes plan.

The Note, which is conciliatory, informs Germany that the Cologne zone cannot be evacuated until the disarmament conditions have been fulfilled.

headline: SOVIET PROTEST. / CHINESE EASTERN RAILWAY. / UNFRIENDLY ACTIONS?
text:
Soviet Government circles are reported to be very perturbed at the Chinese continued disregard of the Soviet demand for the dismissal of non-Soviet officials of the Chinese Eastern Railway.

They also accuse China of exerting anti-Soviet influence, for example in negotiating a lozen with Japan for the purpose of constructing a line from Taoman to Tsitsihar, which is inimical to the interests of the Chinese Eastern Railway.

The Soviet Press reports that the Chinese military authorities have requisitioned 400 waggons for the transport of war material to the Soviet frontier at Pogranitshnaja.

headline: HEAT WAVE. / AMERICA'S SWELTERING ORDEAL.
text:
FATAL RESULTS.

A heat wave has swept the country from the East to the Middle West.

There have been six deaths in Chicago, three in Cleveland and three in New York.

Nine people were drowned at Milwakee when seeking relief from the heat.

Two men in Missouri were flung out of a motor car by the force of a storm and killed.
