headline: OUTLOOK GRAVER / NORTHERN TROUBLE SPREADS.
text:
SERIOUS INCIDENTS.

Week-end reports from many parts of China indicate that the outlook generally is growing graver.

headline: OUTLOOK GRAVER.
text:
The situation is unchanged. The removal of negotiations from Shanghai to Peking has not caused any outward excitement.

It is reported that the Japanese have handed in a Note of protest as regards the affair at Kiukiang; on June 18, but both the Chinese and Japanese authorities are maintaining complete secrecy.

The Union of Labour, Commerce and Education, which came into being in consequence, of the events of May 30, have decided to insist on the continuation of the strike of shops, despite the decision reached at the meeting of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, which decided that the banks should re-open on Sunday.

headline: Terror Gang.
text:
The students yesterday terrorised the shopkeepers, bankers, and members of the Chamber of Commerce in connection with the decision to re-open the banks and shops to-day.

Two special meetings were held in the Chamber yesterday, at which the extremists contended that foreigners would view the re-opening as a sign of weakening. The business members pointed out that the closing of the banks and shops was not materially affecting the foreigners but was causing tremendous Chinese losses, instancing that enormous supplies of tea and cocoons were piling up in Shanghai, which were at present unfinanceable and not movable.

Yesterday morning the meeting resolved to postpone the opening until June 24. Last night's wholly rescinded the resolution of June 19, and resolved to postpone settlement day until the end of the lunar month, namely July 21.

headline: Chairman Attacked.
text:
During the discussions, the extremists bitterly attacked Yu Ya-ching, the Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, charging him with having received $500,000 from the Imperialists to re-open the banks and shops.

Yu Ya-ching vehemently denied this. He hurried to Shanghai from Peking, and since worked day and night in the interests of China and her people. He had not influenced the voting, and he had sufficient money for his few remaining years on this earth.

The attack on Yu Ya-ching silenced other solid business men, and the rescission was carried by a huge majority.

While a definite split between the business members, and the extremists has not occurred, each group is attempting to justify itself, and the outcome will depend largely on the attitude of the Chinese Government.

headline: More Bluster.
text: Delegates, representing 48 colleges, met at the Law College this morning. They sent a deputation to interview the Foreign Minister and War Minister, this afternoon, demanding severance of diplomatic relations with Britain and the impeachment of the Hankow Tupan. The situation, however, at least outwardly, is becoming quiet. There are no signs of the boycott or strike. Numerous students have left for their homes during the past week.

headline: Chungking Trouble.
text:
A message from Chungking yesterday, states that after student agitators worked up popular excitement, rioters on the 17th. attacked foreign customs, employés and assaulted Britons on the streets, though none were seriously hurt. Meanwhile a demonstration occurred at the British Consulate, where the rioters-threatened-the-consular Chinese stuff. The Consul, thereupon, requested the city commandant to furnish a consular guard and restore order. As there was no response, the Consul evacuated the Consulate and went aboard a gunboat.

He sent messages to all Britons, advising them quickly to assemble on the gunboat. The community, on June 18, found accommodation at the riverside, under the protection of gunboats where they are remaining. Order has

been restored in the city, but excitement has not subsided. It is unsafe for foreigners to appear in the streets, though no danger is apprehended under present circumstances. The British Consulate is damaged to an extent unknown, and troops are now guarding it. At Chungking, as at many other centres the rivalries of the militarists have proved an important factor in the situation. Leaders, who are inclined to restore order feared popular ill-will and held aloof at a critical period.

The Foreign Office Note, in reply to the Powers' note regarding the riots against foreign sentiment in China, states that the accounts of different incidents given therein are not in accord with the local Chinese authorities' reports.

The Note gives a lengthy Chinese version of the recent occurrences. It says the Hankow British Volunteers suddenly opened fire on an entirely unarmed crowd and the British authorities should assume full responsibility for their violent action.

At Kiukiang, during an altercation between the police and a small number of workmen, fire suddenly broke out at the Taiwan Bank. During the confusion at the time of putting out the fire slight damage was "caused" to sundry articles in the British and Japanese Consulates. Such damage was accidental. Regarding the killing of a British subject at Shanghai, the Note says that he was outside the Settlement, where the Municipality has built roads without China's consent. The motives of the criminals have not been ascertained. It is regrettable for the above reasons that the incident occurred.

headline: Peking "Stands Firm."
text:
The Note goes on to say that with the exception of the killing of a British subject at Shanghai all the incidents happened as a result of failure to obtain a prompt and fair settlement of the Shanghai case.

There never existed any anti-foreign tendency.

Since the Shanghai occurrence, the Government has issued mandates ordering the people to exercise self-restraint, and has instructed the provincial authorities to maintain order. In view of the present circumstances, the Government hope the Ministers of the Powers will promptly settle the Shanghai case, then the present indignation will be appeased and- excitement subside. The Note, in conclusion, declares "I declare the stand I have taken in the previous protests will be insisted upon."

headline: The Chinese View.
text:
Responding to the diplomatic commission's statement, the Chinese delegation have issued a statement in which they express the belief that a permanent basis of settlement could only be achieved by solving certain questions which have been sources of misunderstanding between the Chinese and foreigners in Shanghai, including the rendition of the Mixed Court, the amelioration of conditions of labourers and the participation of Chinese ratepayers in the Municipal Council.

These points were presented at the first meeting when it was intended to apply for authority to discuss them. But, at the subsequent two meetings, the commission evinced a desire to shift onto the Chinese authorities, the responsibility for indirect causes which led up to the shooting. The commission further stated that not having authority to deal with questions of an international nature it must leave immediately for Peking. The conference was thus brought to an end: The Chinese delegation much regrets that its sincere efforts hitherto have failed to bring about a satisfactory solution.

The statement is signed by Messrs. Tsai Ting-kan, Cheng Chien and Tseng Tsung-chien.

headline: Need For Prayer.
text: At the annual meeting of the conference of British Missionary Societies, a resolution was passed recording the conviction that an urgent need exists for prayerful study of various movements underlying the present situation in China. The Conference considers that the true solution can only be found by mutual confidence and conciliation resulting from a patient and sympathetic investigation of the difficulties with which China at present is confronted as a nation.

headline: From Afar: EDINBURGH, June 20.
text:
Over a thousand delegates, representing sixty countries, attended the opening of the World Women's Christian Temperance Convention. The Conference opened with a devotional session, at which delegates from South Africa, Australia, Denmark Canada, India and China gave short addresses.

Miss Tinling from Shanghai said that in the present trouble the Chinese should not be blamed for the effects of Bolshevik influence. The rest of the world was threatened with the same changes. The Chinese were only doing what mobs do elsewhere.

headline: Shanghai Position.
text:
Shanghai is quiet, but there is no cessation of anti-foreigo propaganda. The decision to reopen the banks and shops is favourably affecting the general situation; but merely reflects the necessity of the Chinese to end the phase of the situation causing them much severer losses and inconvenience than foreigners.

The shipping strike, which is a strong anti-foreign weapon, is not weakening. Strikers are beginning to kidnap Japanese employees who are taken to Chapei, robbed and beaten and only released on payment of money and promises to quit employment.

A wireless from Chinkiang says the strikers have resolved that coal will not be sold to British or Japanese.

No danger is now apprehended t Anking.

At Swatow anti-foreign demonstrations continue.

At Foochow an anti-Japanese boycott has been decided upon but no date has been fixed.

Ample Strike Funds.

The extremists are not concerned in the deadlock, for sufficient funds for strike purposes continue to flow in from China and abroad.

The strikers' programme includes a huge demonstration in the native city to-morrow, which together with the growing activities of organised bands of ruffians, is giving rise to additional precautions. Chang Hsue Liang is bringing a second brigade to Shanghai of Fengtien soldiers and is taking up strategic positions in the vicinity of the native city.

The vernacular papers all published Mr. Chamberlain's speech, some commenting on it as nonsense, and others treating it impartially.

headline: Chungking Situation.
text:
The position here is improving. Foreigners are remaining across the river. The other Yangtze ports, and Peking and Tientsin are quiet. The Chinese Delegation has been ordered to Peking.

Message From The Pope.

The University professors recently solicited the Pope's support in the Shanghai affair. The Pope empowered Mon-signor Constantini, the Apostolic Delegate to China, to signify his sympathy with the great Chinese people and keenly deploring the shedding of fraternal blood and praying that concord and order would soon be restored in a spirit of mutual understanding, according to the principles of justice, equity, and Christian charity.

headline: Fengtien Troops Mutiny.
text: The 3rd Fengtien Regiment mutinied at Chensin, on the Peking Mukden line, damaging the station. The gendarmerie commandant of a neighbouring town has sent a detachment to round up the multi-neers.

headline: Outroges Continue. SHANGHAI Tura
text:
The strikers yesterday afternoon attacked the wharf coolies coaling the Blue Funnel liner Pootung. Messrs. Butterfield and Swire's assistant compradore, intervening, aroused the ire of the strikers who set upon him and chased him to the river-side, where failing to reach a sampah, he fell in and was drowned.

A Briton, Mr. Moalem, a driver of the Volunteer Machine Gun Co., was going home in uniform last night by way of Lord Lane when he was struck between the shoulders and the neck with a meatchopper. He was seriously wounded and taken to Hospital.

[A message received later in correction of the foregoing states that it was the younger brother of the Holt's Wharf compradore who was killed, not Messrs. Butterfield & Swire's compradore]

No damage resulted from the wharf incident which was quickly over. A British warship is protecting the wharf to-day.

Mr. Moalem is progressing satisfactorily.

headline: China Replies to Powers. PEKING June 21
text:
Replying at last to the Powers' note, China maintains her original attitude that nearly all the trouble is due to the conflagration at Shanghai for which the Powers are responsible.

The communication adds that the death of Mr. MacKenzie on June 146, occurred outside the Settlement where the Municipality had built roads without the consent of China.

headline: CHINESE
text:
EXTRAORDINARY INCIDENT

About a hundred young Chinese invaded the Chinese legation this evening, overpowered the porter, cut the telephone wires, locked the doors and gained admission to the private room of the Chinese Minister, whom they threatened with violence and forced him to sign a series of documents, including a proclamation assuring the Chinese people that he sympathised with the struggle against the foreign Imperialists. text: The Norwegian Aeronautic Association says that Amundsen has not made any statement regarding his future plans.

headline: KOWLOON WEDDING.
text:
The Rosary Church, Kowloon, was the scene of a pretty wedding yesterday; the parties being Frederico Muria Gutierrez, only son of Mrs. Milvinin of Shanghai, and Margaret Frances, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. F. H. Barnes of 3 Lyemun Villas, Kowloon.

The bride was given away by her father and was tastefully attired in white georgette with silver trimmings. Her two attendants the Misses Annie and Agnes' Barnes, wore dresses of mauve crepe morocain and pink crepe morocain respectively and the bride's mother was dressed in beige crepe morocain.

The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. Father G. M. Spada and Mr. A. A. R. Botelho and Mr. J. W. Barnes were the bridegroom's sponsors. Mr. O. Baptista was at the organ and suitable solos were rendered by Mr. E. G. Aquino.

The reception held at the Club de Recreio was largely attended and after receiving the congratulations there of many friends the happy couple left for Repulse Bay. Next week, they are to leave by the Empress of Asia for Shanghai.

Paris, June 21.—The "Petit Parisien's Berlin correspondent reports that the British Charge d'Affairs called on Herr Stresemann and emphasised the importance the British Government attaches to the proposals in the French note in regard to security. He declared the note formed the best possible starting point in the negotiations between Germany and the Allies.—Reuter.

Rome, June 20.—The Chamber by 274 votes to 42 adopted a Bill relating to the dismissal of State officials. The Minister of Justice said officials will be asked to embrace the Fascist faith. No official could feel offended, thereat. The law would only affect small groups of would-be politicians who infested the Ministries. An amendment to exclude magistrates from the scope of the law was defeated, Signor Mussolini declaring that the purification of all departments was imperative. No exceptions could be made.—Reuter.

headline: 一
text: Berne, June 20.—With regard to the British and Dutch gold standard measures, the Board of the National Bank states it must maintain the Swiss exchange rate between gold points and the dollar rate. Furthermore the exportation of gold must be facilitated, in this sense, namely, general authorisation of export of unworked gold, must be granted insofar as applicants are able to prove they had imported a like quantity.—Renter.

headline: Santiago de Chile. June
text:
Santiago de Chile, June 21.—In order to stop Soviet propaganda in Chile the Government has ordered that the Russian ship Vorovsky shall not be allowed to enter Chilean ports.—Reuter's American Service.

Moecow, June 21.—The Russian Batic fleet made for the open sea this morning for manoeuvres, with Admiral Frunze abroad a battleship.

Painlevo will early raise a question in the Chamber raising Parliamentary immunity in respect to two Communist leaders, who are deputies, to enable prosecution.

Tangiers, June 20th—situation in the Western Spanish Zone is becoming serious. The Rif contingents are concentrating at various points along the Court Torcan Larache line.—Reuter.

headline: MRS. LANGTRY.
text:
THE DUKE AND THE WATER-LILIES.

"In The Days I Knew" by Lady de Bathe or Mrs. Langtry (to give her the name by which the London of her glorious youth knew her so well) provides here a wealth of good stories and interesting recollections of the great figures in the social world.

Hers is a most entertaining book. Almost from the hour of her first appearance in England as a young bride she became the vogue and was photographed, painted, and worshipped for her extraordinary beauty. The eighth Duke, of Devonshire, who was not usually susceptible on my admiring the lovely coloured water-lilies reposing in marble pools, drenched his clothes pulling them out as an offering, as also the gorgeous liveries of the footmen into whose arms he flung them, and who strewed our brougham with such quantities of the dripping blossoms as to make the latter conveyance rather molster than was convenient.

Simplicity was the note of Mrs. Langtry's life in her first season: Through all this procession of opera, dinners, and balls I wore, extraordinary as it may sound to members of my sex, my one black evening gown, the creation of Mme. Nicole, the fashionable dress-maker of St. Heliers, Jersey.

headline: MET THE PRINCE.
text:
The black frock became the rage, and so with everything she wore:

One morning I twisted a piece of black velvet into a toque, stuck a quill through it, and went to Sandown Park. A few days later this turban appeared in every milliner's window labelled "The langtry Hat." It was very embarrassing and it had all come about so suddenly that I was bewildered.

At her first meeting with King Edward, then Prince of Wales, she says:

I was immensely interested in watching the Prince, and soon realised that, while good-natured and pleasant to everyone, he preserved his dignity admirably; in fact I decided that he would have been a brave man who even at this little intimate supper-party, attempted a familiarity with him. His affability to servants was well known to all who entertained him.

Queen Victoria appears to have looked askance at her. A portrait of her was bought by Prince Leopold, who hung it over his bed in Buckingham Palace, where it remained until one day when he was ill, the Queen went to see him. She evidently did not approve, for I was told she then and there took it down, standing on a chair to do so.

headline: DONKEY IN BED.
text:
With various Princes she indulged in amusing pranks. Thus at a friend's house at Cowes:

One night a donkey was hoisted to the bedroom of the son of the house as a surprise for him—a proceeding in which both the aforesaid Princes took part. I believe they dressed him up and put him in bed, though how to keep him there must have puzzled them.

She tells a charming story of Disraeli:

He remarked quizzically, "What can I do for you?" As it happened to be just before the Ascot Races—a meeting where women like to wear fresh, beautiful frocks, I answered jokingly, "Four new gowns for Ascot," on which he laughed, patted my hand, and said: "You are a sensible young woman. Many a woman would have been made duchess in her own right."

An amusing passage in these lively memoirs is where she tells of an attempt to dye her hair raven black, at the advice of the Austrian Crown Prince Rudolph:

It met with enthusiastic approval on the part of the artist who had achieved the innovation. But, alas! after several washings it became yellow again, with the added glory of heliotrope-zebra-like streaks. The Viennese dye had only worked partially.

headline: GOLF WEDDING. / MR. ROGER WETHERED MARRIED.
text:
CHAMPIONS PRESENT.

Crowds assembled outside St. Margaret's Church, Westminster, on April 29, for the wedding of Mr. Roger Wethered, England's foremost amateur golfer, and Miss Elizabeth Cavendish Bentwick, niece of the Duke of Portland.

Save for Lord Charles Hope who was best man, Mr. Cyril J. H. Tolley who was one of the ushers, Miss Joyce Wethered (the groom's sister and Britain's lady champion) and Mrs. Willock Pollen, the golfing element was absent.

Miss Wethered missed the Surrey women's championship to be present.

headline: HOME BOXING.
text:
LATEST NEWS.

London, May 1.

Elky Clark knocked out Young Johnny Brown in the last round of a 20-round main event at the Albert Hall last night, after a thrilling contest at terrific pace.

Clark is the flyweight champion of Britain but the title was not involved as the midgets fought at 2 lbs. over the limit.

[There is well-founded gossip that the winner may try conclusions for world honours with Pancho Villa who recently gave an exhibition at the "Star," Kowloon, while on his way to the U.S.A.]

Johnny Brown, elder brother of the flyweight and the bantam-champion of Britain, won from Andre Routis (118 lbs. champion of France) in a 15-round bout at 121 lbs., the Frenchman being disqualified for hitting low when well ahead on points in the fifth round.

Bombardier Billy Wells, the ex-champion heavyweight, staged another come-back and was knocked out by Jack Stanley (Deptford) in the 3rd round after going down for a count of eight.

headline: BALLOON RACE.
text:

. CHANNEL DESCENT.

The French balloon Grand Charles competing in the Gordon Bennett Race, descended into the Channel and sank. The occupants were picked up exhausted and taken to hospital.

The French balloon Picardie landed at Anneville in the Department of Manche.

The Belgian balloon Belgica piloted by de Muyter, who has won the Gordon Bennett Cup outright for the past three years, has landed near Quimper.

The German steamer Vaterland wirelesses that she picked up the American balloon Goodyear-the-Third off Ushant last evening. The crew were saved.

headline: SHANGHAI TROUBLE.
text:
TODAY'S HARLIER CABLE

The first trial was resumed in the Mixed Court to-day of seventeen rioters, twenty-nine forfeiting their bail. Lengthy evidence was taken all day long.

Mr. Harry Westridge, a China Inland Missionary, gave evidence that he witnessed occurrences on the afternoon of May 30, which he recounted in minute detail.

Asked whether he considered the shooting necessary, he replied that as a missionary he hated shooting, but if he had been the officer of the law responsible for the station which was attacked he would. There was no option. He believed there was no evidence to show that the students had any personal feeling against the police and vice versa.

Asked whose fault the shooting was, he replied that it was a misfortune. If the events related had happened in England the result would have been, the same. It was the students not the police who were looking for trouble.

Doctors Muir and Chen gave evidence that they examined the wounded and dead rioters. Their opinion was that the bullets entered the bodies from the front or obliquely. One body was hit in the back of the head. It is believed that he was killed at the New World Theatre on June 2. The case was remanded until to-morrow. Bail was offered to all the accused

headline: Chang Tso Lin's Attitude. PEKING. June 9
text: The vernacular papers report that Feng Yu-hsiang has issued a circular supporting the student agitations, also that he has wired to Chang Tso-lin urging that the militarists co-operate with each other and the people to obtain rights for the Chinese. Chang Tso-lin is reported to have replied agreeing with these sentiments, but it is believed that the General is merely desirous of showing sympathy with the popular movement and does not intend any anti-Foreign action.

headline: Settling Down
text:
Apart from the shipping strike, Shanghai continues to settle down. The bakers resumed work this morning. Some shops have reopened, and domestics are returning to work.

No riots have occurred in the river-ports but much unrest is reported. Women and children refugees from Kiukiang will arrive in Shanghai to-morrow. Consular reports from Chungking state that students are agilating, but two commanding Generals assure the Consuls that they will maintain order and guarantee the safety of foreigners.

H.M.S. Hawkins has put in at Woosung. Her departure for Singapore has been postponed indefinitely.

A. P. C. Offices Wrecked.

Rioters wrecked the offices of the Asiatic Petroleum Company at Taiyuanfu.

headline: Peking Student's Demands PEKING. June 0.
text:
The Students' Union here continues to pass extreme resolutions demanding inter alia that all ricsha 'collies' in the Legation quarter should strike, that Anglo-Japanese employed by the Government for Chinese firms should be dismissed, that the telegraph and water should be cut off from the Legation quarter, that the Government should despatch troops to Shanghai, and that Chinese should leave foreign employment.

So far there are no signs that any of these measures are being put into operation, and the suggested boycott also appears to be ineffective.

headline: A Japanese View.

The Cabinet agreed that a more practical step as regards the riots was impossible until the joint Investigation Committee's report was received.

text:

headline: BRIGHTER BANKS / ARMCHAIRS AND BOOKS FOR CLIENTS.
text:
Banks are to be made brighter. Ordinary people usually leave banking premises as quickly as they can. They are oppressed by the melancholy opulence. Now this is to be changed, and the Midland Bank, Limited, will go down to banking history as pioneers.

To make their clients feel thoroughly at home they have opened a reading and writing-room and a ladies' rest-room at their handsome new branch in Piccadilly.

The step is one which will be welcomed by business men. In the beautifully panelled reading and writing room, furnished in the early Georgian style, customers can transact business, write letters, or pass a quiet hour in reading.

"Ample facilities are available in the shape of literature," the bank announces. At one end "of the room is a counter where officials will attend to the requirements of clients.

The ladies' room is decorated in green and gold, the walls are of plaster panelling, while the general design; "electrolier and furniture are all early Georgian.

This “reform” bank stands on the site of the old Vestry Hall of St. James, and is so built that it makes an admirable foil to Wren's church, which the master builder himself considered one of his best contrived churches. A notable feature of the bank is a magnificent Georgian ceiling designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens.

To mark the opening the Midland Bank, Limited, have published a quaintly-bound and illustrated brochure, Landmarks in Piccadilly, for which type purchased in 1672 by Bishop Fell for the Oxford University Press has been used.

headline: ALL RED.
text:
The Chiefs of Gambia expressed themselves when they closed their address to the Prince of Wales with the words, "We are black. We cannot speak or write English, but we are English." I am reminded (says an "Evening Standard" writer) of a story told me by a friend who happened to be in the East at the time of Queen Victoria's death. Going to the memorial service on that occasion he met a Chinese acquaintance, of whom he asked why he was there.

The yellow-skinned British subject replied, "You English—me English. Both alike—All red inside."

headline: THE QUEEN'S DOLLS'
text: Lord Stevenson said that the Queen's Dolls House at Wembley made £38,764, and had been visited by 1,617,556 people. I wonder how many of these visitors really saw the Dolls House (says an "Evening Standard" writer.) For my part, each time I made the circle I became more anxious to be allowed to get up close and spend an hour examining the amazing details. As most visitors probably felt likewise, the moral is that the magnificent total could still further be increased if it may time.

headline: A "NATIONAL JOKE"
text:
DEFENCE OF THE ALBERT MEMORIAL.

For some time I have felt rather sorry for the Albert Memorial, writes Kathleen O'Brien in the Daily Chronicle. From being a National Monument it has somehow passed into a National Joke. Now I find it quite reasonable to joke about a solemn thing that everyone else takes seriously. But to joke about a solemn thing that everyone else jokes about, too... no, that is sheer bullying. I am suddenly and perversely moved to pity. I find I must instantly take its part. It was in this spirit of compassion that I went and had a close look at the Albert Memorial.

headline: A DETAILED STUDY.
text:
You know, there are things about the Albert Memorial, if you honestly look for them. For one thing, to see it properly you stand with your back to the Albert Hall, so that the enormous posters announcing contiguously a performance of the "Dream of Gerontius" and a puglistic bout between Bert Hammerjaw and Kid Basheye are temporarily powerless to inflict their yellow pain. Wherefore the site of the Memorial at least must command our respect. Then let us look (as the guidebooks say) at the figure groups seated at the four outer corners of the base.

Who is this dauntless woman seated on a ferocious bull, with no more sign of nervousness than if she were riding down the Strand on a bus? Ha! Europa, of course. The Big Four are seated at her feet—no, not that Big Four; these are, obviously, Britannia with her trident, Italia with her lyre and palette, France and Germany—er—by the way which is France, and which Germany? One has a book and the other a sword, but that is little to go by. Neither can you go by their faces, for in feature and expression the might be twin sisters, which I am nearly sure is incorrect. However, let us not be fussy fussy about details.

headline: THE INTREPID LADY
text:
Next, America. America, intrepid lady, rides on a bison, with its head down; as if about to butt something. Another intrepid lady, one of America's daughters, is hitting the bison on the head with a nasty-looking stick. "I'll learn you to butt my mother!" she is saying. A man at her side has set down rather suddenly on an astonished lion, which he has completely flattened out. Its claws dangle helplessly in the air. Another standing lady, with a lamb's fleece over her shoulder, offers a bunch of, I think, rhubarb, to an indignant man in a hat and nearly nothing else, who is rightly refusing it. He is holding a rifle in readiness in case his wife offers him rhubarb any more.

Africa comes next. Egypt sensibly rides a camel, which, though possibly old-fashioned, is a far more reliable-steed than these new-fangled bulls and bisons. Near her is a wise man with a note-book in his hand, a kind of hassocky thing—or is it a bale of merchandise? And is his book the Precepts of Ptah-Hatep or a cash account book? Beside the camel a rather "school-marry" person shakes her, finger at a negro who is making faces at her behind Egypt's back. Don't do that, you naughty, rude boy!" she says severely, "after all the pains I've had educating you, too!"

And last, Asia. An elephant nearly as large as the lady who is seated on him has rather ignobly collapsed. You see it is not only the weight of his rider that oppresses him. There is a conquering young man with a far-away expression leaning against the elephant's ribs and sticking the point of his shield into the elephant's side, regardless of the pain he must be inflicting on that dumb, faithful creature. Round the other side a visionary is seated rupt in dreamy contemplation, with his foot very near the elephant's tail. I consider it a great tribute to the remarkable powers of concentration possessed by the visionary that he can retain that serene, placid expression with a justly irritated elephant well within kicking distance. I couldn't.

GREAT MEN'S GRIEVANCES. Now consider the marble relievos of great men at the hasement of the memorial.

Homer, at the centre, touches his lyre, to which listen Dante, on the one hand, and Shakespeare, his tunic trimmed with the now fashionable row of buttons on the other. Pythagoras is saying to Virgil in a disgusted voice, "Just look here! They've only put half of me in! But I suppose you can't expect a nation of shopkeepers to appreciate philosophy!" A little further along, Haydn searches a newspaper anxiously, to know what came home in the 3.30. Purcell closes his ears, with dignity, on an altercation over a document between Tallis and Lawes. Michael Angelo, tired of standing, leans on Raphacl's chair. "Might let me sit down for a bit!" he grumbles, "I don't know what these young people are coming to!" Benzaleel is being rude to Hiram, who won't let him see now much he has in his

headline: IN CHINESE EYES. / GENERAL HSU ON LONDON
text:
In a signed article in the Daily Express General S. T. Hsu, head of the Chinese Mission, now in London to study our economic and political institutions, expresses his admiration of the ladies of London and of the limbs of the law who control the street traffic. The former he describes as "like lotus petals swaying in the wind," and the latter as "marvellous fellows."

London, he says, is to me such an incomprehensible multitude of people that I am overwhelmed by her enormity. I have been in your mighty capital for so little time that my impressions will not yet form themselves. But in my journeyings through her wide, open streets I have cast an eye on her beautiful ladies, her smart guardians of her law, her traffic extraordinary, and some of her marvellous buildings, and these have pleased me. Not yet have I had the honour of pausing in front of the Cenotaph, but I hope soon to be accorded the privilege of placing a wreath of flowers on the tomb of your illustrious dead.

I consider the ladies of London are elegantly attired, of most graceful carriage, and that their demeanour is quiet and modest. As they walk they look like lotus petals swaying in the wind. In China we say that the beauty of a pure and good woman shines like the beauty of a pearl, and that the grace of her carriage and her movements is heavenment. I think of this when I see the wives and daughters and sisters of London citizens, so beautiful, so modest, so full of grace.

Unhappily, it has not been my inestimable joy to meet and hold discourse with these fair daughters of the West, but from my observations I can see that many of them are also highly accomplished and of a great knowledge. It is said that they are as fortunate in the world of commerce as in the smaller world of the household to which in ancient times they were dedicated. Here they are different from my women, who still give an undivided attention to the homes of their husbands.

It is my invariable custom to study the relation of women to society, nor I consider that they exercise a wide influence on politics. These eminent, highly-born men who are so fortunate as to have cultured wives who are intellectual companions and intelligent help-meets to them and good mothers to their children are blessed indeed.

headline: WAKEFULNESS
text:
For your policeman I have nothing but praise. He is a marvellous fellow, for he does nothing at all! And yet I know that it is he who has made the London traffic the orderly, docile organism it is. He only seems to do nothing. Actually it is that white-gloved hand of his that has accomplished everything. I can appreciate perfectly the difficulty of regulating such a big and tremendous traffic. It is a pity and a shame to say so, but during the last four or five years since I have left the city the traffic control in Peking has become worse than before.

Your streets impress me with their cleanliness London is said to be a city of fog and grime. Yet everywhere I see bright, shining cleanliness, and—at this time—marvellous splashes of green. The parks, the quiet, dignified little squares, and the trees in the yards of the ancient churches all make London green and beautiful to me.

I went in a motor-car to Aldershot, where I was entertained to luncheon by Lady Chetwode, the honourable wife of the general commanding your troops in that town. Her home was a pattern of gentle grace and kindly dignity, and she a pattern of hospitality.

As we moved along in the motor-car, through your country roads, I was profoundly moved by that quality of the English spring of which our travellers have so often spoken. It was like the gentle waking-up of the earth child after the slumber of the long, dark winter months.

All about me in your mighty capital I can feel the tradition of centuries, but it possesses also that same spirit of wakefulness which I observed in the country, and which must make it for ever completely different from the slumberous age-old cities of the Orient.

text:
(mean) to anchor in the stream. (In the Back Reach) off the Macao Ports. If the armed boats were fleeing, from the Communists they must have fired to disarm suspicion. However, it may be that they feared an by the Yunnanese and decided to take up a position further away from action. headline: Critical Position.
text:
The exasperation of the Cantonese at the arrogance of the hired Yuhnanese and Hunanese troops who were brought to Canton by the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen to enable him to oust General Chen (Chiung-ming (Chan Kwing-ming) has led to an outbreak of fighting.

While still protesting loyalty to the principles of Sun Yat-sen and the Kuomintang (Kuomintang) party, the Yunnanese Generals Yang' Hsi-nin (Yang Hsi-man) and Lau Chun-wan have demanded that the authorities order the cessation of troop movements on the East and North Rivef districts; otherwise, they will take measures to resist.

The authorities have replied denouncing their insubordination, dismissing them, and appointing General Chu Pei-teh (Chu Pui-tak) acting Commander of the Yunnanese forces.

This is virtual to a declaration of war. Yang Hsi-nin has seized the Governor's 'yamen', the telephone and telegraph offices, and the electric light plant.

The Yunnanese and Cantonese are entrenched on opposite sides of the Canton River.

The Yunnanese control the whole of the Canton side, while the gunboats under the Canton authorities command the river. The Canton authorities chiefly depend on the Whampon cadets who are trained by Soviet officers.

The foregoing message needs explanation in certain places.

Explanation in certain places. It is not the Yunnanese and Hunanese who are ranged against the Cantonese Communists. The Hunanese no longer exist as a fighting force, having been scattered while trying to make their way out of the province of Kwangtung when Dr. Sun was still alive. The Kwangsi merciennaries are the allies of the Yunnanese.

Similarly, General Lau Chun-wan (also spelt Lau Tsun-wan) is not Yunnanese; he commands the Kwangsi army.

Chu Pui-tak also commands a Yunnanese following but he is loyal to the Communists and is their main strength in their stronghold at Honam, the island immediately facing Canton city.

No news has been available from Canton since the time of the night-boats leaving yesterday afternoon as telegraphic communication has been suspended.

This morning, it was gathered that no wireless message had come down from the British gunboats off, Shameen, but that a report had been received to the effect that there had been a general lull in the fighting since yesterday afternoon and up to this morning.

So far, no untoward incident to any foreigner has come to light although those resident in the eastern suburb are inconvenienced through martial law being enforced by the Kwangsi mercenaries and the danger of fighting breaking out there, as the eastern approach is an important strategic point.

There are eight foreign men-of-war at Cantón, viz., the British gunboats, Moth, Tarantula and Cicala, an American sloop and the U.S.S. Pampanga, two French boats and a Japanese man-of-war. Our Canton correspondent reports that General Fan Sheksang, formerly the strong man of Canton, has returned to the city from the West River. Hitherto, the Communists have been counting on his help, or at least his neutrality, but now it is stated

that he has "rejoined his old colleagues:

Mr. Sun Fo (Dr. Sun's son and former Mayor of Canton) went up to Canton as a peacemaker but judging by results, he must have failed. He returned to Hongkong last night.

The Sai On, Kinshan and Paul Beau brought down full complements of refugees last night, the ships being full long before the hour of sailing. As a precaution; the river steamers in Canton had steam up all day yesterday.

The general strike is still in existence and not a cargo boat could be seen in the anchorage yesterday. The river steamers are not carrying any cargo for Canton. This strike is part of the Communist attempt to cut off Canton economically and thus drive the mercenaries out.

Feeling between Cantonese and non-Cantonese in Hongkong ran high on the water-front last night when the river-bonds were leaving for Canton.

Two Yunnanese who were being jostled and threatened by a large crowd, mostly of wharf-coolies were happily taken care of by Mr. W. H. Edmonds of the Public Works Department. Mr. Edmonds was passing in his motor-cycle and saw what was happening. To a "China Mail" reporter, the strangers professed in Southern Mandarin that they were not soldiers but were merchants who had fled from Canton. With two Indian constables bringing up the renr. Mr. Edmonds eventually made a way for the two men who walked behind the motor-cycle and made their way home under Mr. Edmonds's protection.

(From Our Own Correspondent.) Carlton, Sunday.

Developments are also reported from the Eastern River and the Canton-Kowloon Railway. The Yunnanese, of course, make out that they have got to grips with General Hsu Shung-chi's. Cantonese vanguards and defeated several hundred of them in the neighbourhood of Shek Pai, a railway station.

I am also informed that the Yunnanese are securing labour for the railway and that their trains will be working.

Interviewed, by the "China Mail" yesterday: a "Cantonese official who has just arrived from Swatow stated that most of General Chan Kwing-ming's former subordinates are joining General Hsu's anti-mercenary army. Their explanation is that Dr. Sun is dead, Chan Kwing-ming is now out of the field, so the Cantonese should unite against the common enemy since the old feud has expired.

General Hsu is reported to be preparing a march on Canton and the danger of a flank or rear attack from pro-Chan forces, has decreased considerably. Commanders Hung Leuk and Yeung Kwan-yu, former subordinates of Chan, are now embodied in Hsu's army. Ngai Bong-ping has returned to the Kuomintang 'fold and has been appointed Defence Commissioner of the West River, stated the official, with the Civil Governorship when the cause is won.

headline: LORD CURZON / CASTLES FOR THE NATION.
text:
The "Daily Mail" understands that the late Marquis Curzon of Kedleston has left two historic ruins. Tattershall Castle; Lincolnshire, and Bodiam Castle, Sussex, to the nation.

Tattershall Castle, near Withm, is thought to have been erected about 1440. In September, 1911 it was feared that the famous fireplaces would be sent to the United States. They were taken to London, but Lord Curzon, who bought the castle a little later “to save it from being knocked to pieces,” recovered them.

In June 1912 they were returned to their home on decorated lorries which passed beneath triumphal arches. Lord Curzon was in the procession, and his carriage was drawn by ropes by the viliagers.

Bodiam Castle, near Hastings built in 1386, has been described as one of the most beautiful and interesting ruins in England.

It was bought by Lord Curzon in 1917.

The ruins consist of round towers at the angles with five square ones between them, and the great gateway is flanked by two square towers.

An automatic revolver found on a heap of sand at the back of the Kowloon Fire Station was handed over to the Police by Mr. M. Murphy, overseer of the Y.M.C.A, building.

A lamp trimmer on the s.s. On Lee was arrested yesterday for the unlawful possession of 100 tins of opium, one revolver, and 50 rounds of ammunition.

headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The strike is spreading to the French Concession. This morning's estimate of the strikers was 250,000, but a number of staffs resumed work today, including the foreign cable companies and Commercial Pressemployees—also 600 workers at the Japanese Dah Koong Mills, and 500 men at the Riverside power station.

The defence is continually being strengthened, approximately 1,500 marines and blue-jackets have been landed from three British, one French, and one Italian cruiser. Seven American destroyers and ten gunboats (British, Japanese and French), in addition to 400 American marines are due to morrow

The absence of riots and the resumption of the workers' indicate that the students are losing their grip of the situation, while the arrival of the Peking Commissioners, whose mission is only to investigate should help to clear the atmosphere.

The wide nature of the student disturbances is further shown by a Hankow message of Friday, which says that 20,000 students are agitating and distributing anti-Foreign leaflets. The Chinese authorities have so far prevented any big demonstrations; the movement began at Hankow on May 25.

headline: Tientain Parade
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
Tientsin, June 6.—A party of 1,000 students demonstrated in the Native City yesterday afternoon and this morning. There was no incident; the streets are heavily guarded by police, reinforced by Fengtian soldiers.

Professors joined the students who made speeches demanding the restoration of Dairen, boycott of the British and abolition of the Concessions.

Marshall Chang Tsc-lin has assured the Police Chief that he will back every effort to maintain order and assume full responsibility in the event of the Peking Government countermanding police measures.

headline: Widéspread Agitation
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
Numerous student strikes and demonstrations are reported in many cities throughout the country, but no disorder is reported except at Chinkiang where the police station was wrecked. There were no casualties.

Arrangements are being made to despatch a foreign warship to Chinkiang. Chief Executive Tuan Chi-jui's headquarters have issued a circular telegram to the Provinces, stating that Government has lodged strong protests with the Diplomatic Body as regards the Shanghai shootings; and also sent Messrs. Tsai Ting-kan and Tseng Tsung-chien to Shanghai to investigate.

The telegram advises the merchants and students to attend to their own business and await a settlement.

headline: Boycott Urged
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The Cabinet met this morning. It is unofficially reported that they decided to issue a mandate somewhat similar in terms to the Chief Executive's circular telegram. The students held a large demonstration at Tienan Men this afternoon, at which they decided to march to the headquarters of the Chamber of Commerce, surround the building and compel the Chamber to carry out an Anglo-Japanese boycott.

The students surrounded the Chamber of Commerce this afternoon, but were refused admission. Finally a party of student delegates were admitted who urged the inauguration of a strike, a boycott and other measures.

The Chamber practically refused their demands but promised to give a further reply tomorrow.

headline: Powers' Note.
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
After a lengthy meeting this morning of the Ministers of the Powers interested, Signor Cerruti (Italian Minister and Doyen of the "Corps Diplomatique") this evening handed the following Note to the Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs:

I have the honour, in the name of my colleagues and myself, to acknowledge receipt of the Note, dated June 4, which Your Excellency addressed to me, relative to the disorders in Shanghai

While remarking that the reports received by the Chinese Government are incomplete, since they do not mention several attacks against foreigners, my comrades and myself prefer to reserve judgment until the arrival of full details.

To this end, the diplomatic representatives concerned have decided to send a delegation to Shanghai without delay, to study the situation on the spot and submit a report.

I wish at all events, to de-

clare, that the Foreign Authorities of the International Concession, far from having assumed the violent attitude which the Chinese Government attribute to them, have preserved the greatest self-control as proved by the fact that during the past four days—despite numerous provocations—no serious incident has occurred in Shanghai.

I wish to renew the assurance, already given verbally, that the Police of the International Concession have always had instructions to use their arms only if attacked and in imminent danger.

headline: Tatsuta" Sails.
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The Navy Office states that H.I.J.M.S. "Tatsuta" sailed this afternoon for Shanghai. She carried 200 marines.

Four more destroyers have been despatched to Shanghai from Sascho, while two others have been sent from Formosa to Canton.

Signor Cerruti (Italian Minister), this afternoon, handed to the Wachiaооц а second Note, in which it was announced that the Powers are sending a delegation to Shanghai on June 8, to investigate and report.

It is announced that the members of the delegation will be: M. S. Tripier, Counsellor of the French Legation.

Mr G. G. M. Vereker, Secretary of the British Legation.

Mr. E. Gerry Greene, First Secretary of the American Legation.

Mr. Shigemitsu, First Secretary of the Japanese Legation. M. de Schooten, Secretary of the Belgian Legation.

Signor G. Scaduto Menola, Secretary of the Italian Legation.

The Senior Consul this afternoon replied to the Foreign Commissioner's notes of May 31 and June 1, on the subject of the recent disturbances in Shanghai. He recapitulated the main facts of the riots, instancing the deliberate attacks on the police, from which it could be seen that the police action was very different to the Commissioner's version. The question of the propriety of the police action is one which should be raised in the course of legal proceedings; when those arrested are tried. There also will be as a matter of course an investigation by the authorities concerned into the action of the police. Besides which competent courts stand ready to deal with any complaints.

The Settlement authorities naturally assume full responsibility for the action taken for the maintenance of order, but remind the Commissioner of the grave responsibility of the local Chinese authorities in respect to anti-foreign agitation, conducted beyond the limits of the Settlement, to which these regrettable occurrences may largely be attributed.

headline: Chinkiang Outbreak
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The British Consul-General at Chinkiang, near Nanking, tele-graphed to-day: There are riots

in the Concession; can the Navy send assistance?" To which the following reply was sent: "American Admiral last evening wirelessed to an American warship, proceeding up river to put in at Chinkiang."

Later messages stated that the situation was serious. Rioting students had wrecked three houses in the Concession, the Chinese Police, told off-protect foreigners, proving absolutely useless. The rioters carried on joyfully until the Commanding Chinese brought his own troops to the scene, four hours after the Consul General had asked for assistance.

The General restored order and the foreign women and children returned ashore from the boats on which they had taken refuge but a message to night says that the situation is again serious.

The U.S.S. Paul Jones is now due at Chlnkiang and H.M.S. Woodlark should reach there on Monday.

headline: Home Labour Views
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The Council of the Independent Labour Party has issued a statement, sympathising with the alleged oppressive conditions introduced by foreign capitalism into the Far East. It asserts that under the British Flag in the Foreign Concession at Shanghai children of five years of age and upwards are working night and day shifts of twelve hours for seven days weekly, for twopence a day.

The Labourites demand the immediate application of labour legislation worthy of European standards; also the withdrawal of armed forces. The Council protests against the foreign occupation of Chinese cities.

LONDON, June 7. Discussing the trouble in the Far East, the "Observer" says that China cannot long be denied fiscal

autonomy, which is already enjoyed by India. A general re-adjustment in the relationship between the

Western Powers and China is imperative.

China is no more proof against the contagion of her national consciousness and self-respect than the other great countries of the East. The task of the Powers is to give the new spirit it's direction and outlet.

headline: End in Sight?
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The morning papers think that the end of the strike is within sight. There is certainly a remarkable change in the general atmosphere. The Chinese in the streets are beginning to fraternise with the Volunteers.

This is mainly due to the impending departure from Peking of diplomatic representatives, which will lead to the discussions by which the Chinese invariably expect to settle troubles big and small, when momentary excitement has passed.

The situation is still very delicate; however, and little would be required to revive the fires of racial antagonism which the extremists are continually fanning. An outstanding feature of the riots has been the loyalty to the Municipal Council of the Chinese Volunteers, despite the bitter attacks of the vernacular papers, while only 100 out of 1,600 Chinese police failed to withstand the strain of the continual viuperation heaped on them at every point by the strikers.

The arrival at Chinkiang of the U.S.S. Paul Jones last night synchronized with the abatement of the riots, which will apparently not be renewed.

To day's reports state that the situation is quiet. A short wireless message says that students are working up a strike at Kiukiang. There are no details.

That the local student situation is outwardly quiet is largely due to the Tupan of Hsiao-yaonan to day issuing two proclamations, the first to the Chinese and foreign citizens of Wuhan and the second to the educational commissioner and the police. He directed the maintenance of peace. The commissioner also issued a proclamation to the students to the same effect.

headline: Peking Mandate
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The Government issued a mandate last night stating that patriotic citizens had attempted to demonstrate at Shanghai and some had been killed and others wounded, at which the Chief Executive was greatly afflicted. He had asked the Waichiaopu to protest strongly, and had sent delegates of high standing to Shanghai to carry out negotiations to find who was responsible. The Government always protects the interests of the people. All must follow the right channels and work together at this time of difficulty.

The students did not obtain much satisfaction at the Chamber of Commerce yesterday evening, so they proceeded to the Bankers' Association, where they only found one secretary.

They made the usual demands for a boycott etc., and also demand-ed that funds be sent to assist the Shanghai strikers.

The Bankers' Association are meeting to-morrow to consider the demands. Things were very quiet to-day and there were no demonstrations.

headline: Further Peking Note.
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The following is a translation of another Note sent by the Wachiaopu to the Italian Minister, M. Cerruti, as Senior Minister of the Interested. Powers, this evening, "concerning the bloody affair at Shanghai":

I had the honour to address to Your Excellency on the 1st inst. Note in which I begged you to give urgent necessary instructions to the Consular authorities at Shanghai to immediately free those persons who had been arrested and to act in concert with the Special Commissioner for Foreign Affairs, there to hinder the eventual return of similar cases.

Contrary to my expectation, new reports of an inauspicious character continue to reach me, according to which the police of the International Settlement on the 1st inst. again fired on the people, of whom three were killed and eighteen wounded, whilst the persons arrested have not all been freed. Other reports state that most of the victims were shot in the back without any agents of the police having been killed or wounded, which proves that the shooting was quite unjustified.

The violent attitude of the authorities of the International Concession, which has excited the discontent of the general public, creates the gravest consequences, notably the declaration of strikes by the merchants and workers in Shanghai.

From a respect for the elementary principles of humanity, and as the authorities of the International Concession are

entirely responsible, I am forced to address again to Your Excellency the most energetic protests. Moreover, I beg Your Excellency to communicate the above to the Ministers of the interested Powers, and to send without delay the most urgent instructions to the Contular authorities at Shanghai to cease immediately the practice of firing in order to avoid any further effusion of blood.

headline: RULE OF THE WAVES. / BRITAIN'S GREAT EXAMPLE.
text:
Admiral Plunkett, addressing the 93rd. reunion of the New York University, after presenting to the University a 12 inch mortar used by Admiral Faragut in the Civil War as a niemoral to the students of Alumni who died in the great war, hauded Britain's rule of the waves to which he attributed the avoidance of war in the past. He declared that future peace lay in the adoption of this standard of eternal vigilance.

The British consul-general, Sir Harry Armstrong, representing Sir Thomas Lipton, presented the University with the must of Shamrock IV. He made a speech expressing the faith and power of Britain and the United States to establish world peace.

headline: Many Striker

text: Peking, June 6.—Students all over the country are organising strikes and demonstrations but the only disorder is in Chinkiang, where the Police Station was wrecked without casualties. A foreign warship is being despatched thither. Professors have joined in the demonstration at Tientsin, where speeches were made demanding the restoration of Dairen, an anti-British boycott and abolition of concessions.—Reuter.

headline: LUCKY ARREST: / ARMED ROBBERY FOILED. SMART WORK.
text:
A Chinese constable attached No. 7 Police Station (West Point effected a smart arrest on Friday night and thus foiled the well-law plans of a gang of men to rob Chinese house at the junction of Sassoon Road and Pokfulam Road. The raid was timed to take place after the street traffic had stopped. The movements of one member the gang, who was on his way, meet his confederates, called investigation from the constable patrol duty, and a search result in a dagger and some wire bear found on him. The arrested ms subsequently made a statement the police in which he alleged the the dagger was given to him by other man and that they were go to Pokfulam to commit an arn robbery. Soon afterwards the others were also arrested.

The same night another Club was arrested at Queen's Road TV following the discovery of a dog hidden in his shoe. This man made an admission to the Ed that he was proceeding on an awful mission.

The two principal figures these arrests are being charged the Central Magistracy by R sional Inspector Peter Grant.

headline: MAKING MISCHIEEF. / STUDENT AGITATORS URGE BOYCOTT. HANKOW HOTBED.
text:
Student agitators are still making mischief in the North, several of them having now gone to Hankow to attempt to promote a boycott, presumably against British goods.

A few hours later, a breadman employed by Hall and Holtz was stopped at the same place, and relieved of 12 loaves of bread.

Although the thieves in both these cases took the articles to the Chinese Fire Station, officers on duty there, who were interviewed by members of the Municipal Police, denied all knowledge of the incidents.

A number of students tried to seize 20 cattle which were on their way to the French Slaughter House, but desisted on the approach of a party of naval men who escorted the cattle to the settlement.

A Reuter telegram from Peking of June 14. says:—

"General Feng Yu-hsiang, interviewed by the "Ching Pao," declared that in case of hostilities against Britain he would be the first in the field. He said that China need not fear England, which had a big Navy but only a small Army."

We do not for a moment suppose General Feng ever said such a thing, but the invention is interesting, remarks the "North China Daily News."

A “North China Daily News” correspondent writing from Chetoo on June 8 says: — I will just mention that the situation is not so pleasant. The Chinese are demonstrating. They are marching through the streets by hundreds, carrying banners and shouting: “Kill the foreigner,” etc. So far no damage has been done to foreign property but no one knows what the situation will be to-morrow. I did my work all day among some Chinese firms and did some fairly good business. I called on a few foreign firms but had very few results. They seem to be worried about the present disturbance and it is indeed difficult to talk business to men when their attention is attracted by shouting mobs in the street: There has been no violence to foreigners as yet but the police told me to go inside when a mob of ruffians passed by. I think that patrols may be sent ashore from the American men-of-war to-night and if so perhaps the day will be quiet.

headline: Hankow Quiet.

text:
A feature of the local situation, which remains quiet, is the unchecked publication of grossly misrepresented reports regarding Shanghai and other places by the Chinese papers.

Two students have arrived here from Shanghai. Their intentions include an attempt to promote a boycott.

About ten student agitators have also arrived from Peking.

An interview between the Consular Body and Tupan Esaio Yao-nun is being held this afternoon.

Shanghai presented an almost normal appearance on Saturday in that most of the shops in various parts of the Settlement, including Nanking Road were open to some extent, if not entirely, for business. The markets, which have been a point of attack on the part of the agitators and students, were open, with the exception of the meat shops—flowers and garden produce could be seen everywhere, at Hongkew also.

At Arts and Craft all workmen, 450 in number, have resumed their labours, while at Kelly & Walsh's western plant none have returned. Of the Settlement laundrymen, no less than 1,500 refuse to work.

Numerous instances of thieving and rice snatching took place during the week end. On Saturday a gang of coolies assailed two wheelbarrows on Dalny Road and made off with 30 bags of rice. In the Wayside district another gang made off with one sack.

headline: STAR THEATRE. / TREAT FOR MUSIC LOVERS.
text:
The enterprisag management of the Star Theatre has engaged two artistes of world-wide repute who will appear for one night only—on Sunday next. These are Modle Lena Ambiose, soprano and Senor Scamuzzi, late of the Italian Grand opera company. Both are well known in the Colony. Middle Ambiose has a Soprano voice of delightful sweetness, range, and clarity. Scamuzzi—is Scamuzzi! This artist caused a furore on each of his appearances. He has not only a voice but a personality. The mind wanders to "The Barber of Seville," "Carmen," and "Rigoletto" when thinking of Scamuzzi. Both artistes will render selections from Grand opera. There is sure to be a great welcome awaiting these two incomparable artistes.

According to this morning's Chinese papers, the "China News," (the vernacular paper which was raided by the Police some days ago and has since suspended publication) is to be republished by permission of the authorities.

Three Chinese were remanded for one week when charged before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy yesterday with the alleged murder of another Chinese at Wongneichong village. The body of the murdered man was discovered by some coolies below the filter beds on June 1.

headline: FLASH OF FLAME. / STRANGE STORM HEAR CANTON.
text:
TWO LIVES LOST.

FOREIGNERS' NARROW ESCAPE

A whirlwind of intense velocity lasting only two minutes or so struck Tungshan and Taishatau (to the ef the Canton) about 10 45 last night, causing considerable damage and the death of two men by electrocution.

Huts and matsheds were carried away and a part of the German Consulate roof was torn off. Trees were uprooted and the sky was suddenly illuminated by a big red flare. Electric wires snapped, causing the two men's deaths. Foreign residents who had just got back to their homes in this district were reading about the Hongkong storm when many were thrown violently about while windows came tumbling down. It is felt that if the phenomenon had lasted longer much havoc would have been wrought. The strange part about it is that Canton proper were entirely unaware of the sudden storm.

Canton is generally quiet although rumours of a general strike on Monday are in the air. Minor fighting is reported from Fatshan and the North River.

Ngai Bong-ping's resignation is attributed to disagreement with General Hsu Shung-chi and, so the story goes, to some troops lent him by General Leung Hung kai having been disarmed at the hour of victory; by Cantonese colleagues. The latter report is totally unconfirmed.

H. E. the Governor (Sir R. E. Stubbs) will inaugurate the new building of St. Joseph's College on June 24 at 5.30 p.m.

Tokyo, June 18.—The Nichl Nichi reports that the Japanese Construction Company started work on the Taonan Taitahbar� fallway last month and expected to complete it in October—Rentor.

headline: THE RIGHT WAY.
text:
CRITICAL SITUATION CONTROLLED.

GOVERNOR'S FIRM DEALING

On the morning of June 1, just as the students and labour unions of Changsha were preparing for their annual demonstration connection with the "Six-One" (June 1) movement, when it was proposed to commemorate and make demands in connection with the anniversary of the unfortunate affair on the Bund here in 1923 when marines from a Japanese gunboat, in their effort to clear the dock of a violent mob and permit the landing of passengers and freight from a steamer of the Nisshin Kaisha, shot into the crowd and killed a man, the news came to hand of the serious rioting on May 30, in Shanghai, writes a "North China Daily News" correspondent. News that the police had fired into the crowd and that nine students had died caused tremendous consternation and a great outburst of nationalistic feeling. Processions were started at once and for a day or two Governor Chao made no attempt to repress them.

headline: EXCITEMENT HIGH.
text:
By June 4, when word had come of later disturbances in Shanghai and of further shooting, the excitement was running fairly high. Schools that had been parading the streets in connection with the June first celebration now held meetings—that is, the Student Unions did—and other meetings of a violent sort were called in the hall of the Educational Association.

The leaders of the movement calling for retaliation soon organized what is to be called "The Tsing-Hu. (Tsingtao-Shanghai) Cruel Killing Snow Shame (Vengeance) Association." Included in the leadership of this organization are students and labour leaders as well. Every sort of radical proposition has been made, most of them copying the proposals made in Shanghai, for death penalties on the officers that did the shooting in Shanghai on May 30, for the removal of British consular officers; for a complete boycott against the British and Japanese; etc. In many of the schools agitated meetings have been held, usually ending in the taking of a solemn oath by the students body to work here after body, soul and spirit, for the sake of China; and for the enforcement of a complete and permanent economic boycott against Britain and Japan.

headline: AMERICA DRAGGED IN.
text:
Those who watched these developments in school after school came to believe that it would not be long before other countries would be mentioned by name and included in the attack. By the morning of June 6, when word came of an incident in Shanghai on June 3, when American volunteers were fired upon near the New World Theatre, and police action had again become necessary America was also proclaimed as one of the nations to be found guilty. The telegrams here all said that the American Troop had opened fire with a machine gun and had "killed numberless persons." All sors of rumours of impending violence then spread over the city. The governor had already, on June 4, put up a strong proclamation, condemning the shooting in Shanghai on May 30, as unhumanitarian, but urging students and all others to refrain from acts of violence, so as not to give the foreigners any opportunity for incrimination and for retaliatory acts. He proposed severe measures for those who should be found disturbing law and order. This proclamation had had a decided effect until the afternoon of June 6, when the news of the American volunteers reached Changsha.

Before long a girl was found at the gate of the Educational Association, weeping and calling attention to a printed poster on the walls, soon put up all over the city to the effect that an engineer, a foreigner, in the employ of the Canton-Hankow railway, had beaten a Chinese to death. Later in the evening a new rumour was started to the effect that another foreigner had killed a Chinese to the west of the city.

The Governor, Incensed at these fabrications of disturbing rumours came out early on the morning of June 9, with a strong proclamation, showing that such statements were false and urging the populace to become quiet. The entire city was in a state of siege on Saturday night, with groups of armed soldiers guarding all the roads, in and out of the city. Word has come that on the night of Saturday. June 6, a mass meeting of labourers was held in the cotton mill on the opposite bank of the river from Changsha city.
